questions.recognition: Growing tumor + hypoxia + vessels = HIF/VEGF.

questions.stem: A patient with acyclovir-resistant HSV has a viral strain lacking functional thymidine kinase. Which antiviral is the best alternative?
questions.hint: No viral TK? Choose a drug that does not need it.
questions.explanation: Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.

optionExplanations.A: Ribavirin is used in selected viral infections but is not the standard rescue agent for TK-deficient HSV.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.
optionExplanations.C: Zidovudine is an NRTI used for HIV.
optionExplanations.D: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza.
optionExplanations.E: Interferon does not bypass the thymidine-kinase activation problem as directly as foscarnet.

questions.takeaway: Foscarnet bypasses thymidine-kinase activation.
questions.recognition: TK-deficient HSV is the classic foscarnet scenario.

questions.stem: An older adult has anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, back pain, multiple lytic lesions, and a monoclonal protein spike. Which cell type is undergoing malignant proliferation?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.
optionExplanations.B: These define classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
optionExplanations.C: Monocytes are not the malignant population responsible for CRAB findings.
optionExplanations.D: These are seen in T-ALL/LBL.
optionExplanations.E: These are myeloid cells and do not explain a monoclonal immunoglobulin syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell malignancy.
questions.recognition: Punched-out/lytic bone lesions plus monoclonal protein are classic.

questions.stem: A respiratory epithelial cell is infected with an intracellular virus. Viral proteins are synthesized in the cytosol. Which antigen-presentation pathway activates cytotoxic T cells?
options: Fc receptor binding → direct CD8 activation
Complement opsonization → MHC class II only
B-cell receptor uptake → MHC class I
Proteasome degradation → TAP transport into ER → MHC class I
questions.explanation: Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: CD8 T cells recognize peptide-MHC I, not Fc receptor-bound antigen.
optionExplanations.B: Complement can enhance uptake but does not define the endogenous MHC I pathway.
optionExplanations.C: This is the classic exogenous-antigen pathway for CD4 T cells.
optionExplanations.D: BCR-mediated uptake generally feeds MHC II presentation.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.

questions.takeaway: Endogenous antigen → proteasome/TAP/MHC I → CD8.
questions.recognition: Virus made inside a nucleated cell should trigger MHC I.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man has kidney failure while taking a drug cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. The volume of distribution is unchanged. Which pharmacokinetic parameter will increase?
questions.explanation: Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.

optionExplanations.A: Renal failure decreases clearance.
optionExplanations.B: The elimination rate constant falls when clearance falls relative to Vd.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.
optionExplanations.D: Affinity is pharmacodynamic and does not change because of renal failure.
optionExplanations.E: Renal clearance does not inherently raise absorption or bioavailability.

questions.takeaway: Lower clearance means longer half-life when Vd is constant.
questions.recognition: Renal failure + renally cleared drug should make you think accumulation and prolonged half-life.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer experiences profound spiritual and existential distress about meaning, mortality, and separation from a faith community. Which team member is best suited to address this concern?
questions.hint: Match spiritual distress with spiritual care.
questions.explanation: Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.

optionExplanations.A: This is a technical radiation-therapy role.
optionExplanations.B: A dietitian focuses on nutrition and intake.
optionExplanations.C: Physical therapy targets mobility, strength, and deconditioning.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.
optionExplanations.E: Pathologists establish diagnoses from tissues and laboratory specimens.

questions.takeaway: Pastoral care addresses existential and spiritual concerns.
questions.recognition: Do not send a meaning-of-life concern to a purely technical service.

questions.stem: During gastrulation, cells migrate through the primitive streak to create the embryo proper. Which cell population gives rise to ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm?
questions.hint: The embryo proper comes from the upper bilaminar-disc layer.
questions.explanation: All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.

optionExplanations.A: The hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic endoderm.
optionExplanations.B: This invasive trophoblastic layer participates in implantation and placental development.
optionExplanations.C: This is a trophoblastic placental layer.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.
optionExplanations.E: This supports extraembryonic structures rather than generating all three germ layers of the embryo proper.

questions.takeaway: Epiblast gives rise to all three germ layers.
questions.recognition: Primitive streak + all germ layers = epiblast.

questions.stem: An affected father has an X-linked recessive disorder. The mother is not a carrier. Which outcome is expected for their children?
options: All daughters inherit the mutant X chromosome
All sons inherit the mutant X chromosome
questions.hint: Remember: fathers give X to daughters and Y to sons.
questions.explanation: A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.

optionExplanations.A: Daughters inherit the paternal mutant X but also a normal maternal X, so they are generally carriers.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.
optionExplanations.C: Sons do not inherit the paternal X chromosome.
optionExplanations.D: Sons receive the father’s Y chromosome.
optionExplanations.E: No son receives the father’s X chromosome.

questions.takeaway: X-linked disorders show no father-to-son transmission.
questions.recognition: If the affected parent is the father, trace his X only into daughters.

questions.stem: The maternal endometrium directly beneath an implanted embryo becomes the maternal component of the mature placenta. Which structure is being described?
questions.hint: Basalis is the “base” under the embryo.
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.

optionExplanations.A: This covers the conceptus on the side facing the uterine cavity.
optionExplanations.B: This is the remaining decidualized endometrium away from implantation.
optionExplanations.C: The amnion encloses the amniotic cavity and fetus.
optionExplanations.D: This forms the fetal component of the placenta.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.

questions.takeaway: Maternal placenta = decidua basalis; fetal placenta = chorion frondosum.
questions.recognition: Questions asking for the maternal placental component point to decidua basalis.

questions.stem: A young adult has hundreds of adenomatous colonic polyps. Loss of which tumor-suppressor gene is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: MSH2 is a mismatch-repair gene associated with Lynch syndrome, which usually does not produce hundreds of polyps.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.
optionExplanations.C: Activating RET mutations cause MEN2.
optionExplanations.D: Germline TP53 mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: BRCA1 is associated mainly with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.

questions.takeaway: FAP = APC loss.
questions.recognition: Polyposis in youth should immediately suggest APC.

questions.stem: Homologous chromosomes separate normally during gametogenesis, but both sister chromatids of chromosome 18 migrate into the same gamete during the second division. At which stage did nondisjunction occur?
questions.explanation: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.
optionExplanations.B: Chromosomes align but do not separate here.
optionExplanations.C: Homolog pairing and recombination occur in prophase I; separation does not.
optionExplanations.D: The segregation error occurs before fertilization.
optionExplanations.E: Anaphase I separates homologs.

questions.takeaway: Meiosis II nondisjunction is failure of sister chromatids to separate.
questions.recognition: If homologs separated normally but sisters did not, the error is in meiosis II.

questions.stem: A malnourished person drinks a large amount of ethanol without eating and later becomes hypoglycemic. Which biochemical change most directly inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis?
options: Increased NADH drives pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate
questions.hint: Think redox state: ethanol raises NADH.
questions.explanation: Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: The central mechanism is the altered NADH/NAD+ redox ratio.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the reason gluconeogenesis fails after ethanol ingestion.
optionExplanations.C: Ethanol metabolism increases, rather than decreases, NADH.
optionExplanations.D: Glucagon instead favors gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Excess NADH diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis.
questions.recognition: Fasting + alcohol + hypoglycemia is a redox problem.

questions.stem: A patient develops hemolytic anemia after a medication becomes attached to erythrocyte membranes and IgG binds the drug-associated cell surface. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.

optionExplanations.A: Type I is IgE-mediated immediate allergy.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.
optionExplanations.C: Type III involves soluble circulating immune complexes depositing in tissues.
optionExplanations.D: Type IV is T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity.
optionExplanations.E: Tolerance prevents immune responses rather than producing antibody-mediated cell injury.

questions.takeaway: Type II antibodies bind cell-surface or matrix antigens.
questions.recognition: Hemolysis from antibodies coating RBCs is Type II.

questions.stem: Drug X has a dissociation constant (KD) of 2 nM at a receptor, whereas Drug Y has a KD of 200 nM. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Drug Y must have greater efficacy
Drug X has greater receptor affinity
Drug X must be a full agonist
questions.explanation: KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.

optionExplanations.A: Higher KD means weaker affinity.
optionExplanations.B: KD reflects affinity, not maximal effect.
optionExplanations.C: Their KD values differ by 100-fold.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.
optionExplanations.E: Binding affinity does not establish intrinsic efficacy.

questions.takeaway: KD measures affinity, not efficacy.
questions.recognition: Do not confuse affinity with maximal response.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin-induced agglutination. Which platelet receptor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.

optionExplanations.A: P2Y12 is an ADP receptor and antiplatelet-drug target.
optionExplanations.B: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia with preserved ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.D: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A rather than giant platelets and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.E: PAR-1 is a thrombin receptor and is not the classic defect here.

questions.takeaway: Bernard-Soulier = GpIb adhesion defect.
questions.recognition: Ristocetin tests vWF-GpIb interaction.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient develops pulmonary nodules and brain abscesses. Culture shows thin branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.
optionExplanations.B: M tuberculosis is acid-fast but does not form the characteristic branching filamentous morphology.
optionExplanations.C: Corynebacteria are club-shaped rods, not branching weakly acid-fast filaments.
optionExplanations.D: Actinomyces is branching gram positive but generally anaerobic and not acid-fast.
optionExplanations.E: Streptomyces is filamentous but does not fit the classic opportunistic weakly acid-fast pulmonary/CNS syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Nocardia is an aerobic, weakly acid-fast branching bacterium.
questions.recognition: Pulmonary infection with brain abscesses is a classic Nocardia pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has pain, anxiety, transportation problems, financial stress, and spiritual distress. Which approach best represents holistic patient care?
options: Allow family members to make all decisions
Postpone nonmedical issues until cancer treatment is complete
Refer every concern away without coordinating care
Integrate physical, psychological, social, cultural, and spiritual needs into the care plan
questions.hint: The answer should address the whole person, not one problem.
questions.explanation: Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.

optionExplanations.A: Patient-centered care prioritizes the capable patient’s own values and preferences.
optionExplanations.B: These issues can directly affect current health and treatment adherence.
optionExplanations.C: Interdisciplinary referrals are valuable, but care must remain integrated.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.
optionExplanations.E: This addresses only one physical dimension.

questions.takeaway: Holistic care integrates multiple dimensions of health.
questions.recognition: If several nonbiologic factors are affecting care, the best answer is integrated care.

questions.stem: An oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus from a respiratory specimen does not ferment glucose, maltose, lactose, or sucrose. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Diplococcus + oxidase positive + no sugars = Moraxella.
questions.explanation: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.

optionExplanations.A: N lactamica can ferment glucose, maltose, and lactose.
optionExplanations.B: Pseudomonas is an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod, not a diplococcus.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.
optionExplanations.D: N gonorrhoeae ferments glucose.
optionExplanations.E: N meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose.

questions.takeaway: Moraxella is asaccharolytic.
questions.recognition: Carbohydrate utilization is a useful way to distinguish Moraxella from Neisseria.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is given an oral solute that crosses an epithelial membrane through a specific carrier without direct ATP hydrolysis. Transport rises with concentration and then reaches a plateau. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which transport mechanism best fits these findings?
questions.hint: The clue is “down gradient + carrier + saturation + no ATP.”
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses a finite number of carrier proteins to move solute down its electrochemical gradient. Because carrier number is limited, the process is saturable even though ATP is not directly consumed.

optionExplanations.A: Primary active transport directly hydrolyzes ATP.
optionExplanations.B: Simple diffusion is not carrier-saturable.
optionExplanations.C: Secondary active transport couples movement to another ion gradient and can move a solute uphill.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Facilitated diffusion uses a finite number of carrier proteins to move solute down its electrochemical gradient. Because carrier number is limited, the process is saturable even though ATP is not directly consumed.
optionExplanations.E: Endocytosis uses vesicles rather than a saturable membrane carrier for small solutes.

questions.takeaway: Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated, passive, and saturable.
questions.recognition: A plateau in transport rate strongly suggests carrier saturation.

questions.stem: A treatment truly reduces recurrence, but an underpowered study reports no statistically significant difference from placebo. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which quantity is the probability of making this error?
questions.explanation: Failing to detect a true effect is a Type II error. The probability of a Type II error is beta, and statistical power equals 1 − beta.

optionExplanations.A: Power is 1 − beta and represents the probability of detecting a true effect.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the probability of a Type II error.
optionExplanations.C: Alpha is the probability of a Type I false-positive error.
optionExplanations.D: Sensitivity is a diagnostic-test property.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Failing to detect a true effect is a Type II error. The probability of a Type II error is beta, and statistical power equals 1 − beta.

questions.takeaway: Beta is the Type II error probability; power = 1 − beta.
questions.recognition: Underpowered + real difference missed = beta.

questions.stem: An infant develops vomiting, sweating, profound hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly shortly after fruit juice is introduced. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Symptoms begin when fructose/sucrose enters the diet.
questions.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: This causes von Gierke disease and is not specifically triggered by fructose introduction.
optionExplanations.B: GALT deficiency causes classic galactosemia after milk exposure.
optionExplanations.C: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign essential fructosuria.
optionExplanations.D: Galactokinase deficiency primarily causes cataracts.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Hereditary fructose intolerance = aldolase B deficiency.
questions.recognition: Fruit introduction + hypoglycemia + liver dysfunction is the classic pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic pain says, “I may not eliminate the pain, but I am willing to experience some discomfort so I can keep doing what matters to me.”. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which construct is best demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Pain acceptance is willingness to experience pain without allowing it to control participation in valued activities.

optionExplanations.A: Fear avoidance leads patients to restrict activity due to concern about pain or injury.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Pain acceptance is willingness to experience pain without allowing it to control participation in valued activities.
optionExplanations.C: Hypervigilance is excessive attention to bodily sensations.
optionExplanations.D: Catastrophizing focuses on worst-case interpretations and helplessness.
optionExplanations.E: Somatization does not describe this adaptive willingness to function despite discomfort.

questions.takeaway: Acceptance means making room for pain while pursuing meaningful function.
questions.recognition: The key is not giving up; it is acting according to values despite pain.

questions.stem: A healthy sperm reaches the secondary oocyte under normal physiologic conditions. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Where does fertilization most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.
optionExplanations.B: The cervix is part of the sperm’s route but not the usual fertilization site.
optionExplanations.C: The ampulla, not the isthmus, is the most common site.
optionExplanations.D: The blastocyst later implants in the uterus; fertilization usually occurs before arrival there.
optionExplanations.E: The oocyte is released from the ovary before fertilization.

questions.takeaway: Fertilization = ampulla; implantation = endometrium.
questions.recognition: Ampulla is the classic normal fertilization site.

questions.stem: A hypoxic cell develops ATP depletion, ion-pump failure, and marked intracellular calcium accumulation. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme activities most directly worsen structural injury?
options: Glycogen synthase and protein kinase A
questions.hint: High intracellular calcium turns on destructive enzymes.
questions.explanation: Elevated cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes and proteases that degrade cytoskeletal and structural proteins. Calcium also worsens mitochondrial dysfunction.

optionExplanations.A: These are not the main calcium-activated destructive enzymes in acute injury.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Elevated cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes and proteases that degrade cytoskeletal and structural proteins. Calcium also worsens mitochondrial dysfunction.
optionExplanations.C: These do not explain calcium-mediated membrane and cytoskeletal destruction.
optionExplanations.D: These ATP-dependent pumps fail rather than become destructive effectors.
optionExplanations.E: These are not acute effectors of calcium-mediated necrotic injury.

questions.takeaway: Calcium activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases.
questions.recognition: In ischemic injury, calcium is dangerous because it activates degradative enzymes.

questions.stem: A child has normal or elevated IgM but profoundly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgE. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which defect most likely prevents class switching?
questions.hint: IgM high, other isotypes low = class-switch failure.
questions.explanation: T-dependent class switching requires CD40 on B cells interacting with CD40L on activated helper T cells. CD40L deficiency produces hyper-IgM syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. T-dependent class switching requires CD40 on B cells interacting with CD40L on activated helper T cells. CD40L deficiency produces hyper-IgM syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: MPO is a neutrophil microbicidal enzyme.
optionExplanations.C: TAP deficiency impairs MHC I antigen presentation.
optionExplanations.D: C5 deficiency predisposes to Neisseria.
optionExplanations.E: Factor H regulates complement rather than immunoglobulin switching.

questions.takeaway: CD40-CD40L signaling is required for T-dependent class switching.
questions.recognition: Hyper-IgM is the classic CD40L clue.

questions.stem: A child with chronic hemolytic anemia has deletion of three alpha-globin genes. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which abnormal hemoglobin is expected?
options: Hb Barts composed of gamma4 tetramers
questions.explanation: Three alpha-globin gene deletions cause HbH disease. In adults, excess beta chains form beta4 tetramers called HbH.

optionExplanations.A: HbA2 is elevated in beta-thalassemia trait but is not dominant here.
optionExplanations.B: Hb Barts is most severe in four-gene alpha deletion during fetal life.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Three alpha-globin gene deletions cause HbH disease. In adults, excess beta chains form beta4 tetramers called HbH.
optionExplanations.D: HbS results from a beta-globin missense mutation.
optionExplanations.E: HbC is a structural beta-chain variant.

questions.takeaway: HbH = beta4 from three alpha-gene deletions.
questions.recognition: Four alpha deletions give gamma4 Hb Barts; three give beta4 HbH.

questions.stem: A patient has flaccid skin blisters and oral erosions. Biopsy shows acantholysis within the epidermis. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which structure is targeted by autoantibodies?
questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins in desmosomes, causing loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion and flaccid intraepidermal blisters.

optionExplanations.A: Connexins form gap junctions.
optionExplanations.B: Type IV collagen is a basement-membrane component and does not explain intraepidermal acantholysis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins in desmosomes, causing loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion and flaccid intraepidermal blisters.
optionExplanations.D: Hemidesmosomal targets are more relevant to bullous pemphigoid.
optionExplanations.E: Claudins are tight-junction proteins.

questions.takeaway: Pemphigus targets desmogleins.
questions.recognition: Flaccid blisters plus mucosal involvement should make you think pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.stem: A patient with an anaerobic intra-abdominal infection receives metronidazole. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which mechanism best describes its antimicrobial effect?
options: Reactive metabolites damage microbial DNA and cause strand breaks
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is reduced within susceptible anaerobic organisms and generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA, causing strand breaks.

optionExplanations.A: This is not metronidazole’s mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: This is an antifungal mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: That is a beta-lactam mechanism.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Metronidazole is reduced within susceptible anaerobic organisms and generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA, causing strand breaks.
optionExplanations.E: Trimethoprim inhibits DHFR.

questions.takeaway: Metronidazole creates toxic radicals that damage DNA.
questions.recognition: Think anaerobes/protozoa and DNA strand breaks.

questions.stem: A sexually active young woman has cystitis. Culture grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci that are resistant to novobiocin. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Coag negative + novobiocin resistant + UTI = saprophyticus.
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus and a common cause of UTI in young sexually active women.

optionExplanations.A: S epidermidis is coagulase negative but classically novobiocin sensitive.
optionExplanations.B: Group B Streptococcus is catalase negative and CAMP positive.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus and a common cause of UTI in young sexually active women.
optionExplanations.D: S aureus is coagulase positive.
optionExplanations.E: Enterococcus is catalase negative.

questions.takeaway: S saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant.
questions.recognition: Use novobiocin to separate saprophyticus from epidermidis.

questions.stem: A patient has severe hypertriglyceridemia, eruptive xanthomas, and recurrent pancreatitis. Lipoprotein lipase is structurally normal, but its required apolipoprotein activator is absent. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which apolipoprotein is deficient?
questions.explanation: ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II deficiency therefore causes severe chylomicronemia and pancreatitis.

optionExplanations.A: ApoE mediates hepatic uptake of remnant particles.
optionExplanations.B: ApoB-48 is structural for chylomicrons.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II deficiency therefore causes severe chylomicronemia and pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.D: ApoB-100 is structural for VLDL/LDL and binds the LDL receptor.
optionExplanations.E: ApoA-I activates LCAT and is central to HDL metabolism.

questions.takeaway: ApoC-II activates LPL.
questions.recognition: Severe triglycerides + pancreatitis can be LPL deficiency or ApoC-II deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer experiences profound spiritual and existential distress about meaning, mortality, and separation from a faith community. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which team member is best suited to address this concern?
questions.hint: Match spiritual distress with spiritual care.
questions.explanation: Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.

optionExplanations.A: Pathologists establish diagnoses from tissues and laboratory specimens.
optionExplanations.B: Physical therapy targets mobility, strength, and deconditioning.
optionExplanations.C: This is a technical radiation-therapy role.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.
optionExplanations.E: A dietitian focuses on nutrition and intake.

questions.takeaway: Pastoral care addresses existential and spiritual concerns.
questions.recognition: Do not send a meaning-of-life concern to a purely technical service.

questions.stem: An older adult has anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, back pain, multiple lytic lesions, and a monoclonal protein spike. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which cell type is undergoing malignant proliferation?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.

optionExplanations.A: These are myeloid cells and do not explain a monoclonal immunoglobulin syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Monocytes are not the malignant population responsible for CRAB findings.
optionExplanations.C: These are seen in T-ALL/LBL.
optionExplanations.D: These define classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.

questions.takeaway: Multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell malignancy.
questions.recognition: Punched-out/lytic bone lesions plus monoclonal protein are classic.

questions.stem: A tumor becomes hypoxic as it enlarges. Tumor cells increase VEGF transcription and stimulate new-vessel formation. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which molecular change most directly drives this response?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1alpha, which enters the nucleus and promotes expression of adaptive genes including VEGF. VEGF drives the angiogenic switch.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1alpha, which enters the nucleus and promotes expression of adaptive genes including VEGF. VEGF drives the angiogenic switch.
optionExplanations.B: This is a cell-cycle checkpoint effect rather than the hypoxia response.
optionExplanations.C: Hypoxia prevents normal HIF-1alpha degradation.
optionExplanations.D: This would reduce angiogenesis.
optionExplanations.E: This would reduce replicative capacity, not stimulate angiogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Hypoxia → HIF-1alpha stabilization → VEGF.
questions.recognition: Growing tumor + hypoxia + vessels = HIF/VEGF.

questions.stem: An affected father has an X-linked recessive disorder. The mother is not a carrier. Which outcome is expected for their children?
options: All sons inherit the mutant X chromosome
All daughters inherit the mutant X chromosome
questions.hint: Remember: fathers give X to daughters and Y to sons.
questions.explanation: A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.

optionExplanations.A: Daughters inherit the paternal mutant X but also a normal maternal X, so they are generally carriers.
optionExplanations.B: Sons receive the father’s Y chromosome.
optionExplanations.C: No son receives the father’s X chromosome.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.
optionExplanations.E: Sons do not inherit the paternal X chromosome.

questions.takeaway: X-linked disorders show no father-to-son transmission.
questions.recognition: If the affected parent is the father, trace his X only into daughters.

questions.stem: A patient with acyclovir-resistant HSV has a viral strain lacking functional thymidine kinase. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which antiviral is the best alternative?
questions.hint: No viral TK? Choose a drug that does not need it.
questions.explanation: Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.
optionExplanations.B: Interferon does not bypass the thymidine-kinase activation problem as directly as foscarnet.
optionExplanations.C: Ribavirin is used in selected viral infections but is not the standard rescue agent for TK-deficient HSV.
optionExplanations.D: Zidovudine is an NRTI used for HIV.
optionExplanations.E: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza.

questions.takeaway: Foscarnet bypasses thymidine-kinase activation.
questions.recognition: TK-deficient HSV is the classic foscarnet scenario.

questions.stem: A respiratory epithelial cell is infected with an intracellular virus. Viral proteins are synthesized in the cytosol. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which antigen-presentation pathway activates cytotoxic T cells?
options: B-cell receptor uptake → MHC class I
Proteasome degradation → TAP transport into ER → MHC class I
Complement opsonization → MHC class II only
Fc receptor binding → direct CD8 activation
questions.explanation: Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: BCR-mediated uptake generally feeds MHC II presentation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.
optionExplanations.C: Complement can enhance uptake but does not define the endogenous MHC I pathway.
optionExplanations.D: This is the classic exogenous-antigen pathway for CD4 T cells.
optionExplanations.E: CD8 T cells recognize peptide-MHC I, not Fc receptor-bound antigen.

questions.takeaway: Endogenous antigen → proteasome/TAP/MHC I → CD8.
questions.recognition: Virus made inside a nucleated cell should trigger MHC I.

questions.stem: During gastrulation, cells migrate through the primitive streak to create the embryo proper. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which cell population gives rise to ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm?
questions.hint: The embryo proper comes from the upper bilaminar-disc layer.
questions.explanation: All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.

optionExplanations.A: This invasive trophoblastic layer participates in implantation and placental development.
optionExplanations.B: The hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic endoderm.
optionExplanations.C: This is a trophoblastic placental layer.
optionExplanations.D: This supports extraembryonic structures rather than generating all three germ layers of the embryo proper.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.

questions.takeaway: Epiblast gives rise to all three germ layers.
questions.recognition: Primitive streak + all germ layers = epiblast.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has kidney failure while taking a drug cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. The volume of distribution is unchanged. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which pharmacokinetic parameter will increase?
questions.explanation: Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.

optionExplanations.A: The elimination rate constant falls when clearance falls relative to Vd.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.
optionExplanations.C: Renal clearance does not inherently raise absorption or bioavailability.
optionExplanations.D: Renal failure decreases clearance.
optionExplanations.E: Affinity is pharmacodynamic and does not change because of renal failure.

questions.takeaway: Lower clearance means longer half-life when Vd is constant.
questions.recognition: Renal failure + renally cleared drug should make you think accumulation and prolonged half-life.

questions.stem: Homologous chromosomes separate normally during gametogenesis, but both sister chromatids of chromosome 18 migrate into the same gamete during the second division. At which stage did nondisjunction occur?
questions.explanation: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.

optionExplanations.A: The segregation error occurs before fertilization.
optionExplanations.B: Homolog pairing and recombination occur in prophase I; separation does not.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.
optionExplanations.D: Anaphase I separates homologs.
optionExplanations.E: Chromosomes align but do not separate here.

questions.takeaway: Meiosis II nondisjunction is failure of sister chromatids to separate.
questions.recognition: If homologs separated normally but sisters did not, the error is in meiosis II.

questions.stem: A patient develops hemolytic anemia after a medication becomes attached to erythrocyte membranes and IgG binds the drug-associated cell surface. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.

optionExplanations.A: Type IV is T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity.
optionExplanations.B: Type III involves soluble circulating immune complexes depositing in tissues.
optionExplanations.C: Type I is IgE-mediated immediate allergy.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.
optionExplanations.E: Tolerance prevents immune responses rather than producing antibody-mediated cell injury.

questions.takeaway: Type II antibodies bind cell-surface or matrix antigens.
questions.recognition: Hemolysis from antibodies coating RBCs is Type II.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient develops pulmonary nodules and brain abscesses. Culture shows thin branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.

optionExplanations.A: M tuberculosis is acid-fast but does not form the characteristic branching filamentous morphology.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.
optionExplanations.C: Actinomyces is branching gram positive but generally anaerobic and not acid-fast.
optionExplanations.D: Streptomyces is filamentous but does not fit the classic opportunistic weakly acid-fast pulmonary/CNS syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Corynebacteria are club-shaped rods, not branching weakly acid-fast filaments.

questions.takeaway: Nocardia is an aerobic, weakly acid-fast branching bacterium.
questions.recognition: Pulmonary infection with brain abscesses is a classic Nocardia pattern.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has pain, anxiety, transportation problems, financial stress, and spiritual distress. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which approach best represents holistic patient care?
options: Refer every concern away without coordinating care
Integrate physical, psychological, social, cultural, and spiritual needs into the care plan
Allow family members to make all decisions
Postpone nonmedical issues until cancer treatment is complete
questions.hint: The answer should address the whole person, not one problem.
questions.explanation: Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.

optionExplanations.A: Interdisciplinary referrals are valuable, but care must remain integrated.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.
optionExplanations.C: This addresses only one physical dimension.
optionExplanations.D: Patient-centered care prioritizes the capable patient’s own values and preferences.
optionExplanations.E: These issues can directly affect current health and treatment adherence.

questions.takeaway: Holistic care integrates multiple dimensions of health.
questions.recognition: If several nonbiologic factors are affecting care, the best answer is integrated care.

questions.stem: An oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus from a respiratory specimen does not ferment glucose, maltose, lactose, or sucrose. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Diplococcus + oxidase positive + no sugars = Moraxella.
questions.explanation: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.
optionExplanations.B: N gonorrhoeae ferments glucose.
optionExplanations.C: N meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose.
optionExplanations.D: N lactamica can ferment glucose, maltose, and lactose.
optionExplanations.E: Pseudomonas is an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod, not a diplococcus.

questions.takeaway: Moraxella is asaccharolytic.
questions.recognition: Carbohydrate utilization is a useful way to distinguish Moraxella from Neisseria.

questions.stem: Drug X has a dissociation constant (KD) of 2 nM at a receptor, whereas Drug Y has a KD of 200 nM. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Drug X must be a full agonist
Drug Y must have greater efficacy
Drug X has greater receptor affinity
questions.explanation: KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.

optionExplanations.A: Higher KD means weaker affinity.
optionExplanations.B: Their KD values differ by 100-fold.
optionExplanations.C: Binding affinity does not establish intrinsic efficacy.
optionExplanations.D: KD reflects affinity, not maximal effect.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.

questions.takeaway: KD measures affinity, not efficacy.
questions.recognition: Do not confuse affinity with maximal response.

questions.stem: The maternal endometrium directly beneath an implanted embryo becomes the maternal component of the mature placenta. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which structure is being described?
questions.hint: Basalis is the “base” under the embryo.
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.

optionExplanations.A: This is the remaining decidualized endometrium away from implantation.
optionExplanations.B: This covers the conceptus on the side facing the uterine cavity.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.
optionExplanations.D: This forms the fetal component of the placenta.
optionExplanations.E: The amnion encloses the amniotic cavity and fetus.

questions.takeaway: Maternal placenta = decidua basalis; fetal placenta = chorion frondosum.
questions.recognition: Questions asking for the maternal placental component point to decidua basalis.

questions.stem: A malnourished person drinks a large amount of ethanol without eating and later becomes hypoglycemic. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which biochemical change most directly inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis?
options: Increased NADH drives pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate
questions.hint: Think redox state: ethanol raises NADH.
questions.explanation: Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: The central mechanism is the altered NADH/NAD+ redox ratio.
optionExplanations.B: Glucagon instead favors gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.C: Ethanol metabolism increases, rather than decreases, NADH.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.E: This is not the reason gluconeogenesis fails after ethanol ingestion.

questions.takeaway: Excess NADH diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis.
questions.recognition: Fasting + alcohol + hypoglycemia is a redox problem.

questions.stem: A young adult has hundreds of adenomatous colonic polyps. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Loss of which tumor-suppressor gene is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.
optionExplanations.B: Activating RET mutations cause MEN2.
optionExplanations.C: BRCA1 is associated mainly with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
optionExplanations.D: MSH2 is a mismatch-repair gene associated with Lynch syndrome, which usually does not produce hundreds of polyps.
optionExplanations.E: Germline TP53 mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome.

questions.takeaway: FAP = APC loss.
questions.recognition: Polyposis in youth should immediately suggest APC.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin-induced agglutination. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which platelet receptor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.

optionExplanations.A: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia with preserved ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.B: P2Y12 is an ADP receptor and antiplatelet-drug target.
optionExplanations.C: PAR-1 is a thrombin receptor and is not the classic defect here.
optionExplanations.D: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A rather than giant platelets and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.

questions.takeaway: Bernard-Soulier = GpIb adhesion defect.
questions.recognition: Ristocetin tests vWF-GpIb interaction.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain says, “The pain is still present, but I know I can work, exercise, and care for my family even when it hurts.” Which psychological construct is demonstrated?
questions.hint: Confidence in functioning despite pain = self-efficacy.
questions.explanation: Pain self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function and continue valued activities despite pain.

optionExplanations.A: Helplessness is a maladaptive belief that one cannot cope.
optionExplanations.B: Fear avoidance involves restricting activity because movement is believed to cause harm.
optionExplanations.C: Hypervigilance is excessive monitoring of pain sensations.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pain self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function and continue valued activities despite pain.
optionExplanations.E: Catastrophizing involves rumination, magnification, and helplessness.

questions.takeaway: Pain self-efficacy is adaptive confidence, not absence of pain.
questions.recognition: The patient is describing function despite symptoms.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman receives a drug that blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase. Intracellular sodium rises and the transmembrane sodium gradient falls. Which normal transport stoichiometry is directly inhibited?
options: 2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in per ATP
2 Na+ out and 2 K+ in without ATP
3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP
1 Na+ out and 1 K+ in per ATP
3 Na+ in and 2 K+ out per ATP
questions.hint: Remember the classic “3 out, 2 in, 1 ATP” rule.
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+-ATPase hydrolyzes one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+. The unequal charge movement makes the pump electrogenic and establishes the sodium gradient used by many secondary transporters.

optionExplanations.A: This reverses the normal stoichiometry.
optionExplanations.B: The pump is primary active transport and requires ATP.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Na+/K+-ATPase hydrolyzes one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+. The unequal charge movement makes the pump electrogenic and establishes the sodium gradient used by many secondary transporters.
optionExplanations.D: The pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.
optionExplanations.E: This reverses the direction of both ions.

questions.takeaway: Na+/K+-ATPase = 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, 1 ATP.
questions.recognition: Ouabain/digoxin + rising intracellular Na+ should trigger the Na+/K+ pump stoichiometry.

questions.stem: A patient develops diffuse rash, watery diarrhea, and hepatitis several weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. Which immune process is responsible?
options: Immune complexes deposit in the graft
Recipient antibodies attack donor stem cells
Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
questions.hint: Remember the direction: graft attacks host.
questions.explanation: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient tissues as foreign. Skin, GI tract, and liver are classic targets.

optionExplanations.A: Neutrophils are not the principal effector cells of GVHD.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the primary mechanism of GVHD.
optionExplanations.C: This is Type I hypersensitivity, not GVHD.
optionExplanations.D: That describes host-versus-graft rejection rather than graft-versus-host disease.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient tissues as foreign. Skin, GI tract, and liver are classic targets.

questions.takeaway: GVHD = donor T cells attacking recipient tissues.
questions.recognition: Stem-cell transplant + rash + diarrhea + hepatitis = GVHD.

questions.stem: A teenager develops exercise-induced muscle cramps and myoglobinuria. After a brief rest, exercise becomes easier. Lactate fails to rise normally during a forearm exercise test. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: McArdle disease is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Skeletal muscle cannot efficiently mobilize glycogen during intense exercise, causing cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and the second-wind phenomenon.

optionExplanations.A: This causes severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. McArdle disease is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Skeletal muscle cannot efficiently mobilize glycogen during intense exercise, causing cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and the second-wind phenomenon.
optionExplanations.C: This causes a hepatic glycogen-storage disorder rather than exercise-induced muscle symptoms.
optionExplanations.D: Cori disease primarily causes hepatic manifestations.
optionExplanations.E: Andersen disease causes abnormal glycogen and progressive liver disease.

questions.takeaway: McArdle = muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency.
questions.recognition: If lactate does not rise with exercise, think a block in muscle glycogen use.

questions.stem: A cervical biopsy shows severe atypia throughout the full epithelial thickness, but the basement membrane is intact. Which diagnosis best describes this lesion?
questions.hint: Full thickness + intact basement membrane = in situ.
questions.explanation: Carcinoma in situ is full-thickness epithelial dysplasia without invasion through the basement membrane. Breach of the basement membrane defines invasive carcinoma.

optionExplanations.A: Hypertrophy is increased cell size rather than dysplastic epithelial growth.
optionExplanations.B: Hyperplasia increases cell number while preserving orderly architecture.
optionExplanations.C: Invasive carcinoma requires breach of the basement membrane.
optionExplanations.D: Metaplasia is replacement of one mature cell type by another without full-thickness malignant atypia.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Carcinoma in situ is full-thickness epithelial dysplasia without invasion through the basement membrane. Breach of the basement membrane defines invasive carcinoma.

questions.takeaway: Carcinoma in situ has not invaded the basement membrane.
questions.recognition: The basement membrane is the dividing line between in situ and invasive carcinoma.

questions.stem: A child has chronic jaundice, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones, and spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is negative, and a parent had the same condition. Which defect is most likely?
questions.hint: Inherited spherocytes + negative DAT = hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects in RBC membrane-skeleton proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Membrane loss produces poorly deformable spherocytes cleared in the spleen.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects in RBC membrane-skeleton proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Membrane loss produces poorly deformable spherocytes cleared in the spleen.
optionExplanations.B: This produces oxidant-triggered bite cells/Heinz bodies.
optionExplanations.C: This is sickle-cell disease and produces sickled cells rather than hereditary spherocytes.
optionExplanations.D: Warm autoimmune hemolysis is usually DAT positive and not inherited in this pattern.
optionExplanations.E: This is a coagulation disorder, not a hemolytic anemia.

questions.takeaway: Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane-cytoskeleton disorder.
questions.recognition: Always use DAT to separate hereditary from immune spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A clinical trial concludes that a drug is superior to placebo even though there is actually no true treatment effect and the null hypothesis is correct. Which statistical error occurred?
questions.explanation: A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis—concluding that a difference exists when it does not. Its probability is alpha.

optionExplanations.A: Type II error is failure to detect a real effect.
optionExplanations.B: Lead-time bias is a screening-survival artifact.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis—concluding that a difference exists when it does not. Its probability is alpha.
optionExplanations.D: Recall bias involves differential memory of past exposures.
optionExplanations.E: Confounding is distortion by a third variable, not this hypothesis-testing error.

questions.takeaway: Type I error: reject a true null; probability = alpha.
questions.recognition: If the study “finds” an effect that is not real, think Type I error.

questions.stem: A patient with tuberculosis receives rifampin. Which bacterial enzyme is directly inhibited?
questions.explanation: Rifampin binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and inhibits transcription. It is also a strong hepatic enzyme inducer.

optionExplanations.A: Sulfonamides inhibit this enzyme.
optionExplanations.B: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase.
optionExplanations.C: Beta-lactamase inhibitors target this resistance enzyme, not rifampin.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Rifampin binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and inhibits transcription. It is also a strong hepatic enzyme inducer.
optionExplanations.E: Several protein-synthesis inhibitors target the 50S subunit.

questions.takeaway: Rifampin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
questions.recognition: TB drug + orange fluids/enzyme induction often points to rifampin.

questions.stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis develops chalky white deposits within peripancreatic adipose tissue. Which type of necrosis produced this finding?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipases digest surrounding adipose triglycerides. Released fatty acids bind calcium and produce chalky saponification deposits, the classic appearance of enzymatic fat necrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pancreatic lipases digest surrounding adipose triglycerides. Released fatty acids bind calcium and produce chalky saponification deposits, the classic appearance of enzymatic fat necrosis.
optionExplanations.B: This is classically associated with tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.C: This occurs in brain infarcts and many abscesses.
optionExplanations.D: This is a vascular-wall necrosis pattern.
optionExplanations.E: This is typical of ischemic injury in most solid organs.

questions.takeaway: Fat necrosis in pancreatitis reflects lipase-mediated saponification.
questions.recognition: If the stem says chalky white peripancreatic deposits, the answer is fat necrosis.

questions.stem: A researcher analyzes normal decidual leukocytes in early pregnancy. Which population is most abundant?
questions.hint: The dominant decidual immune cell is an innate lymphocyte.
questions.explanation: Specialized uterine natural killer cells are the dominant leukocyte population in healthy early decidua and participate in trophoblast interaction and vascular remodeling.

optionExplanations.A: Plasma cells are not predominant.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Specialized uterine natural killer cells are the dominant leukocyte population in healthy early decidua and participate in trophoblast interaction and vascular remodeling.
optionExplanations.C: Eosinophils are not the major normal decidual population.
optionExplanations.D: B cells are not the dominant decidual leukocyte population.
optionExplanations.E: Neutrophils are important in acute inflammation but are not the dominant normal decidual leukocyte population.

questions.takeaway: Uterine NK cells dominate the decidua.
questions.recognition: Pregnancy-immunology cell-frequency questions usually point to NK cells.

questions.stem: A blastocyst has formed after cleavage and morula stages. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. When does implantation normally begin?
questions.explanation: Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.

optionExplanations.A: Placental and fetal circulation develop after implantation begins.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.
optionExplanations.C: Implantation begins much earlier.
optionExplanations.D: This is far too late.
optionExplanations.E: The conceptus must first undergo cleavage and blastocyst formation.

questions.takeaway: Implantation begins around the end of the first week.
questions.recognition: Blastocyst stage means implantation is imminent.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man takes an oral medication that has a volume of distribution of 50 L, a desired plasma concentration of 8 mg/L, and oral bioavailability of 50%. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What loading dose is required?
questions.hint: Calculate the systemic requirement first, then divide by F.
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.

optionExplanations.A: This underestimates the dose and effectively multiplies rather than divides by bioavailability.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.
optionExplanations.C: This overcorrects for incomplete bioavailability.
optionExplanations.D: This does not follow the loading-dose relationship.
optionExplanations.E: This would be the dose if bioavailability were 100%.

questions.takeaway: Loading dose depends on Vd, target concentration, and bioavailability.
questions.recognition: If oral F is below 1, the administered loading dose must be larger than the systemic requirement.

questions.stem: A patient with invasive fungal disease receives an azole. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which fungal enzyme is inhibited?
questions.hint: Azoles block ergosterol synthesis, not the cell wall.
questions.explanation: Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.

optionExplanations.A: This is a bacterial cell-wall target.
optionExplanations.B: This is the echinocandin target.
optionExplanations.C: Polyenes bind ergosterol rather than inhibiting its synthesis enzyme.
optionExplanations.D: This is inhibited by terbinafine.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.

questions.takeaway: Azoles inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase.
questions.recognition: Membrane sterol synthesis + CYP inhibition = azole.

questions.stem: A malignant cell line takes up large amounts of glucose and converts pyruvate to lactate despite adequate oxygen and intact mitochondria. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which phenomenon is present?
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.

optionExplanations.A: Beta-oxidation degrades fatty acids in mitochondria.
optionExplanations.B: The respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species in phagocytes.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.
optionExplanations.D: Ketogenesis produces ketone bodies during fasting states.
optionExplanations.E: The Cori cycle transfers lactate to liver for gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Warburg effect = aerobic glycolysis.
questions.recognition: FDG-PET works partly because many tumors avidly consume glucose.

questions.stem: A patient develops bite cells and Heinz bodies after taking an oxidizing medication. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which biochemical defect most directly causes the erythrocyte injury?
options: Decreased NADPH production with impaired regeneration of reduced glutathione
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.
optionExplanations.B: This is the mechanism of thalassemia.
optionExplanations.C: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
optionExplanations.D: This causes vitamin B12 deficiency.
optionExplanations.E: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and do not use the TCA cycle.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency impairs antioxidant defense in RBCs.
questions.recognition: Oxidant drug + bite cells/Heinz bodies = G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: Repeated measurements of the same reference sample are nearly identical, but all are consistently 15% above the true value. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. How should this assay be described?
questions.hint: Precise but wrong = reliable, not valid.
questions.explanation: Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.

optionExplanations.A: Sensitivity and specificity describe diagnostic classification, not measurement accuracy/precision.
optionExplanations.B: The assay is precise but not accurate.
optionExplanations.C: Reliability is high because measurements are tightly reproducible.
optionExplanations.D: The measurements are consistent but inaccurate, the opposite pattern.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.

questions.takeaway: Reliability = precision; validity = accuracy.
questions.recognition: Tight cluster away from truth is high reliability, low validity.

questions.stem: A teenager has recurrent meningococcal infections with otherwise normal immune function. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which immune defect is most likely?
options: Deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5-C9)
questions.explanation: Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.

optionExplanations.A: C3 deficiency causes broader susceptibility to pyogenic encapsulated infections.
optionExplanations.B: MPO deficiency does not produce the classic recurrent meningococcal pattern.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
optionExplanations.D: IgE deficiency does not classically cause recurrent Neisseria.
optionExplanations.E: This is a bleeding disorder, not an immune defect.

questions.takeaway: C5-C9 deficiency → recurrent Neisseria.
questions.recognition: Repeated meningococcal infection is the classic board clue for MAC deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient repeatedly misses chemotherapy because of job loss, gasoline costs, and risk of eviction. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which interdisciplinary team member is best suited to address these barriers?
questions.hint: Match the referral to the barrier.
questions.explanation: Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.

optionExplanations.A: A pathologist focuses on tissue and laboratory diagnosis.
optionExplanations.B: A speech therapist addresses communication and swallowing rehabilitation.
optionExplanations.C: A dermatologist treats skin disease rather than primary housing/transportation barriers.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.
optionExplanations.E: A radiation physicist supports technical radiation planning and safety.

questions.takeaway: Social work addresses housing, transportation, finances, and resource access.
questions.recognition: If the problem is access rather than biology, think social work.

questions.stem: A patient has acute leukemia with abnormal promyelocytes, numerous Auer rods, and DIC. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which treatment should be initiated urgently?
questions.hint: Promyelocytes + Auer rods + DIC = APL = ATRA.
questions.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.
optionExplanations.B: Hydroxyurea can lower high leukocyte counts but does not correct the PML-RARA differentiation block.
optionExplanations.C: Erythropoietin does not treat acute leukemia or DIC.
optionExplanations.D: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL and is classically used in CML.
optionExplanations.E: Rituximab targets CD20-positive B-cell malignancies.

questions.takeaway: ATRA is urgent differentiation therapy for APL.
questions.recognition: APL is one of the leukemia diagnoses where immediate targeted therapy matters.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is heterozygous for an autosomal dominant pathogenic allele with 80% penetrance. The partner does not carry the allele. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the probability that their next child will develop the disease?
questions.explanation: The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.

optionExplanations.A: This is the classic affected-child risk for two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder.
optionExplanations.B: This does not correctly combine 50% transmission with 80% penetrance.
optionExplanations.C: This is the transmission probability before accounting for penetrance.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.
optionExplanations.E: This is penetrance among those who inherit the allele, not the overall child risk.

questions.takeaway: Reduced penetrance lowers observed disease risk below genotype transmission risk.
questions.recognition: For autosomal dominant disease with incomplete penetrance, do not stop at 50%.

questions.stem: A sarcoma amplifies MDM2. TP53 is structurally normal, but p53 protein concentrations are markedly reduced. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which molecular event explains this finding?
options: Increased ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of p53
questions.explanation: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.
optionExplanations.B: MDM2 does not primarily suppress BCL2.
optionExplanations.C: MDM2 lowers p53 protein rather than increasing it.
optionExplanations.D: BAX is a proapoptotic p53 target and would not explain low p53.
optionExplanations.E: Reduced p53 lowers p21 induction.

questions.takeaway: MDM2 ubiquitinates p53.
questions.recognition: Wild-type TP53 with low p53 protein suggests excessive MDM2 activity.

questions.stem: A palpable breast mass is firm and irregular. Ultrasound is suspicious, but mammography is negative. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No further evaluation because mammography is negative
questions.hint: Suspicious mass beats a negative screening test.
questions.explanation: A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.
optionExplanations.B: FNA gives cytology but less tissue architecture; core biopsy is preferred for a suspicious solid lesion.
optionExplanations.C: A negative mammogram does not override a suspicious mass and ultrasound.
optionExplanations.D: This would inappropriately delay diagnosis.
optionExplanations.E: Suspicious clinical and ultrasound findings require tissue diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Suspicious solid breast lesion → core needle biopsy.
questions.recognition: Never let a negative mammogram cancel a concerning palpable/ultrasound finding.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent hemarthroses. PT is normal, aPTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing, and factor VIII activity is markedly reduced. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: Deep bleeding + VIII deficiency = Hemophilia A.
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.

optionExplanations.A: vWD more often causes mucocutaneous bleeding and abnormal platelet adhesion.
optionExplanations.B: Hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.
optionExplanations.C: This is a platelet-adhesion defect with giant platelets.
