optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.
optionExplanations.E: Factor XII deficiency can prolong aPTT but usually does not cause clinical bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Hemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency.
questions.recognition: Hemarthroses are a secondary-hemostasis clue.

questions.stem: A newborn has distal intestinal aganglionosis and fails to pass meconium. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which developmental process failed?
options: Migration of neural crest cells into the hindgut
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.

optionExplanations.A: Intermediate mesoderm forms urogenital structures, not enteric neurons.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.
optionExplanations.C: Persistence can produce sacrococcygeal teratoma.
optionExplanations.D: The notochord organizes axial development but does not directly populate enteric ganglia.
optionExplanations.E: Failure causes neural-tube defects, not enteric aganglionosis.

questions.takeaway: Hirschsprung = failed neural crest migration.
questions.recognition: Newborn obstruction + absent ganglion cells is a neural-crest question.

questions.stem: Genetic analysis of a trisomic conceptus shows that both homologous maternal chromosomes were transmitted into the same oocyte. Which meiotic error occurred?
options: Failure of DNA replication in S phase
questions.explanation: Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.

optionExplanations.A: Recombination abnormalities can predispose to nondisjunction but do not themselves describe both homologs entering one gamete.
optionExplanations.B: Postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction generally produces mosaicism.
optionExplanations.C: Replication failure is not chromosome nondisjunction.
optionExplanations.D: Meiosis II errors involve sister chromatids rather than homologous chromosomes.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.

questions.takeaway: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes.
questions.recognition: If the stem explicitly says “both homologs,” choose meiosis I.

questions.stem: A patient develops urticaria, wheezing, facial swelling, and hypotension within minutes of peanut exposure. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which immune mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

optionExplanations.A: This is a Type II mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: This is a Type III mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection rather than causing this immediate allergic syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: This is Type IV hypersensitivity and develops over a longer interval.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

questions.takeaway: Type I = IgE + mast cells.
questions.recognition: Rapid hypotension and wheezing after exposure is anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A newborn with meningitis has beta-hemolytic catalase-negative gram-positive cocci. Hemolysis is enhanced adjacent to Staphylococcus aureus on agar. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

optionExplanations.A: Group A Streptococcus is beta hemolytic but is not CAMP positive.
optionExplanations.B: Enterococcus is typically bile-esculin positive and grows in 6.5% NaCl.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
optionExplanations.D: S pneumoniae is alpha hemolytic and optochin sensitive.
optionExplanations.E: Staphylococci are catalase positive.

questions.takeaway: S agalactiae is CAMP positive.
questions.recognition: Neonatal meningitis plus enhanced hemolysis is a classic GBS clue.

questions.stem: A receptor has constitutive activity even in the absence of ligand. A new drug binds the receptor and reduces signaling below the basal level. Which term best describes this drug?
questions.hint: The key phrase is “below basal activity.”
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.

optionExplanations.A: A positive allosteric modulator enhances receptor responsiveness.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.
optionExplanations.C: A neutral antagonist blocks agonists but does not reduce constitutive activity.
optionExplanations.D: A partial agonist still increases activity above baseline, though less than a full agonist.
optionExplanations.E: A full agonist increases receptor signaling.

questions.takeaway: Inverse agonist = negative efficacy at a constitutively active receptor.
questions.recognition: Constitutive activity plus a drug that lowers the baseline points to an inverse agonist.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated HIV has a CD4 count of 150/µL, progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.

optionExplanations.A: CMV classically causes retinitis, esophagitis, or colitis at very low CD4 counts.
optionExplanations.B: Cryptococcus is a classic cause of meningitis in advanced HIV.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
optionExplanations.D: MAC typically appears at more profound immunosuppression and often causes disseminated disease.
optionExplanations.E: Toxoplasma most classically causes CNS lesions and neurologic findings.

questions.takeaway: Pneumocystis is the classic pulmonary OI below 200 CD4 cells/µL.
questions.recognition: Use CD4 thresholds as pattern-recognition anchors.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is exercising intensely. Cellular ATP falls while AMP rises. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is most directly activated to increase glycolytic flux?
questions.explanation: AMP signals a low-energy state and activates PFK-1, the key committed regulatory enzyme of glycolysis, thereby increasing ATP production.

optionExplanations.A: This is a gluconeogenic enzyme.
optionExplanations.B: AMP inhibits this gluconeogenic enzyme.
optionExplanations.C: This enzyme supports hepatic glucose release rather than glycolysis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. AMP signals a low-energy state and activates PFK-1, the key committed regulatory enzyme of glycolysis, thereby increasing ATP production.
optionExplanations.E: This enzyme catalyzes a gluconeogenic/anaplerotic reaction.

questions.takeaway: AMP activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
questions.recognition: PFK-1 is the high-yield glycolytic checkpoint for low-energy states.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender firm uterus. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.
optionExplanations.B: A partial mole is a triploid abnormal gestation and does not fit this late-pregnancy emergency.
optionExplanations.C: Previa typically causes painless bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Accreta presents mainly as abnormal placental adherence and postpartum hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.E: Cervical insufficiency usually causes painless dilation in the second trimester.

questions.takeaway: Abruption causes painful bleeding and a tender/firm uterus.
questions.recognition: Pain + bleeding + firm uterus is a classic triad.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced illness asks how hospice differs from palliative care. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Palliative care cannot be given during chemotherapy
Hospice and palliative care are identical
Hospice requires expected death within 24 hours
Hospice generally serves patients with an estimated prognosis of about 6 months or less
questions.hint: Hospice is the narrower end-of-life model.
questions.explanation: Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.

optionExplanations.A: Palliative care can be concurrent with disease-directed treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Hospice addresses many physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs.
optionExplanations.C: Palliative care is broader and can occur much earlier.
optionExplanations.D: Hospice is not limited to the final day of life.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.

questions.takeaway: Hospice is generally associated with a prognosis of about 6 months or less.
questions.recognition: Palliative care is broad; hospice has a more specific end-of-life eligibility framework.

questions.stem: A patient develops an intensely pruritic rash 48 hours after nickel exposure. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.
optionExplanations.B: Type I reactions are immediate rather than delayed by 48 hours.
optionExplanations.C: Type III involves soluble immune complexes.
optionExplanations.D: Complement deficiency does not produce contact dermatitis.
optionExplanations.E: Type II targets fixed antigens with IgG/IgM.

questions.takeaway: Type IV = delayed, T-cell mediated.
questions.recognition: Nickel and poison ivy are classic Type IV triggers.

questions.stem: A growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase. GRB2 and SOS activate Ras. Which downstream sequence most directly promotes proliferative gene transcription?
questions.hint: Think of the classic MAPK kinase cascade.
questions.explanation: The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: This is a GPCR pathway.
optionExplanations.B: Smad signaling is associated with TGF-beta receptors and does not proceed through Gq.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.
optionExplanations.D: JAK/STAT is a cytokine-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.E: PI3K signals mainly through PIP3 and AKT, not caspase-8.

questions.takeaway: RTK/GRB2/SOS → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK.
questions.recognition: A Ras question usually wants the MAPK cascade.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman develops right-sided colon cancer. Several first-degree relatives developed colon or endometrial cancer before age 50, and tumor testing shows microsatellite instability. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which DNA repair system is defective?
questions.hint: Family history + right colon/endometrium + MSI = mismatch repair.
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

optionExplanations.A: This is not the pathway responsible for Lynch syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.
optionExplanations.C: NER is associated with bulky DNA lesions and xeroderma pigmentosum.
optionExplanations.D: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks.
optionExplanations.E: BER repairs small altered bases rather than replication mismatches.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome = defective DNA mismatch repair.
questions.recognition: Microsatellite instability is the biochemical fingerprint of mismatch-repair failure.

questions.stem: An infant has severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and marked hepatomegaly. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly = GSD I.
questions.explanation: Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Deficiency causes Andersen disease with abnormal glycogen and cirrhosis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.C: Deficiency causes Cori disease, which is generally milder and preserves gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.D: Deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia.
optionExplanations.E: Deficiency causes McArdle disease with exercise intolerance.

questions.takeaway: Von Gierke = glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.
questions.recognition: If both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis fail at the final step, think G6Pase.

questions.stem: A renal artery thrombosis causes an infarct. Days later, dead renal tubules retain their general architectural outlines despite loss of nuclei. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which pattern of necrosis is present?
questions.hint: Most solid-organ infarcts coagulate; brain liquefies.
questions.explanation: Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.

optionExplanations.A: Caseous necrosis is classically associated with tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.B: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in damaged vessel walls, such as vasculitis.
optionExplanations.C: Fat necrosis occurs in settings such as acute pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.D: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain infarction and many abscesses.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.

questions.takeaway: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture for a time.
questions.recognition: Kidney/heart/spleen infarct = coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: A patient develops jaundice and dark urine after an oxidant drug. Smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.

optionExplanations.A: This causes DAT-positive spherocytic hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: This causes microcytic anemia without oxidant-triggered hemolysis.
optionExplanations.C: This causes spherocytes due to membrane-skeleton defects.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.
optionExplanations.E: This causes microcytosis from reduced beta-globin synthesis.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis.
questions.recognition: Bite cells are a classic post-Heinz-body clue.

questions.stem: A patient with MRSA bacteremia receives vancomycin. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which bacterial structure does the drug bind?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.

optionExplanations.A: This is targeted by fluoroquinolones.
optionExplanations.B: This is inhibited by rifampin.
optionExplanations.C: This is targeted by aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.
optionExplanations.E: This is inhibited by trimethoprim.

questions.takeaway: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala.
questions.recognition: Differentiate vancomycin from beta-lactams: substrate binding versus PBP binding.

questions.stem: A patient has anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, and reticulocytosis after mechanical heart-valve placement. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which additional finding most strongly supports intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.

optionExplanations.A: Ferritin is nonspecific and does not directly identify intravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: Erythropoietin generally rises in response to anemia.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.
optionExplanations.D: This can occur in hereditary spherocytosis but is not the best marker of intravascular destruction.
optionExplanations.E: Splenomegaly is more strongly associated with chronic extravascular hemolysis.

questions.takeaway: Intravascular hemolysis lowers haptoglobin.
questions.recognition: Mechanical hemolysis plus low haptoglobin fits intravascular destruction.

questions.stem: A cancer-screening program detects tumors several years earlier. Five-year survival after diagnosis increases, but cancer-specific mortality is unchanged. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which bias best explains the apparent benefit?
questions.hint: Earlier diagnosis without later death = lead-time bias.
questions.explanation: Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.

optionExplanations.A: Observer bias arises from measurement influenced by expectations.
optionExplanations.B: Length-time bias preferentially detects slower-growing disease.
optionExplanations.C: Recall bias affects remembered exposures.
optionExplanations.D: Selection bias concerns who enters or remains in a study.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Lead-time bias inflates post-diagnosis survival without improving mortality.
questions.recognition: Always compare survival to disease-specific mortality in screening questions.

questions.stem: An older adult has large tense blisters. Biopsy shows the entire epidermis separating from the underlying basement membrane while epidermal cells remain attached to one another. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which structure is targeted?
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.

optionExplanations.A: Adherens junctions link actin cytoskeletons between cells.
optionExplanations.B: Gap junctions mediate cell communication.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.
optionExplanations.D: Tight junctions regulate paracellular permeability.
optionExplanations.E: Desmosomal disruption produces intraepidermal acantholysis and flaccid blisters.

questions.takeaway: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes.
questions.recognition: Flaccid = desmosomes; tense = hemidesmosomes.

questions.stem: A young child has severe microcytic anemia, marrow expansion, skeletal changes, hepatosplenomegaly, and transfusion dependence. Hemoglobin analysis shows very high HbF and almost no HbA. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: High HbF + absent HbA + severe childhood disease = beta-thal major.
questions.explanation: Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.
optionExplanations.B: Sickle trait has HbA greater than HbS and is usually asymptomatic.
optionExplanations.C: HbC trait is generally mild.
optionExplanations.D: Iron deficiency does not produce this hemoglobin pattern or marrow-expansion syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Alpha trait is generally mild microcytosis.

questions.takeaway: Beta-thalassemia major causes severe ineffective erythropoiesis.
questions.recognition: Think of globin composition, not just microcytosis.

questions.stem: A child has impaired phagocytosis of encapsulated bacteria because the organisms are not efficiently coated for complement-receptor recognition. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which complement component normally performs this function?
questions.explanation: C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: C5a is a potent chemotactic and inflammatory mediator.
optionExplanations.B: C9 participates in the membrane attack complex.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.
optionExplanations.D: C1 inhibitor regulates complement/contact activation rather than opsonizing microbes.
optionExplanations.E: C3a is mainly an anaphylatoxin.

questions.takeaway: C3b coats; C3a/C5a inflame; C5b-9 punches holes.
questions.recognition: Encapsulated organism + complement receptor = C3b.

questions.stem: A patient with candidemia receives micafungin. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which fungal structure is most directly disrupted?
options: Beta-1,3-D-glucan component of the fungal cell wall
Ergosterol in the membrane through pore formation
questions.explanation: Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.

optionExplanations.A: Flucytosine metabolites interfere with nucleic-acid synthesis, not beta-glucan.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.
optionExplanations.C: Polyenes bind ergosterol and form pores.
optionExplanations.D: Azoles inhibit this enzyme and reduce ergosterol synthesis.
optionExplanations.E: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase.

questions.takeaway: Micafungin inhibits beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis.
questions.recognition: Candida + micafungin should trigger echinocandin cell-wall inhibition.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man receives a drug by continuous IV infusion. Renal function improves and the drug clearance doubles while the desired steady-state concentration remains unchanged. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What dosing change is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.

optionExplanations.A: Volume of distribution is not a dosing adjustment.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.
optionExplanations.C: Higher clearance lowers steady-state concentration unless dosing rate is increased.
optionExplanations.D: Lowering the rate would further reduce steady-state exposure.
optionExplanations.E: Loading dose depends mainly on volume of distribution and target concentration, not clearance.

questions.takeaway: Maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.
questions.recognition: When clearance changes, maintenance dosing changes; loading dose is tied to Vd.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain says, “My spine must be getting destroyed. It will only get worse, and there is nothing I can do.” The patient spends hours ruminating about the pain. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which psychological construct is most strongly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.

optionExplanations.A: Values-based action involves pursuing meaningful activities despite symptoms.
optionExplanations.B: Acceptance is adaptive willingness to experience pain while functioning.
optionExplanations.C: Pacing is structured activity management.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.
optionExplanations.E: Self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function despite pain.

questions.takeaway: Catastrophizing = rumination + magnification + helplessness.
questions.recognition: “It is terrible and I cannot cope” is the core cognitive pattern.

questions.stem: A breast-fed infant develops vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and cataracts. Urine contains a reducing sugar but the glucose dipstick is negative. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Milk exposure + cataracts + liver disease = classic galactosemia.
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.

optionExplanations.A: Galactokinase deficiency is milder and mainly causes cataracts without severe hepatic disease.
optionExplanations.B: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign fructosuria.
optionExplanations.C: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance after fruit/sucrose exposure.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.
optionExplanations.E: This causes von Gierke disease rather than a milk-triggered galactose syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Classic galactosemia = GALT deficiency.
questions.recognition: If cataracts are accompanied by severe systemic toxicity, distinguish GALT deficiency from isolated galactokinase deficiency.

questions.stem: A sperm penetrates the zona pellucida and fuses with the oocyte membrane. Cortical granules are released immediately afterward. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the main purpose of the cortical reaction?
questions.hint: One sperm in; lock the door.
questions.explanation: The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.

optionExplanations.A: Capacitation occurs before the sperm reaches and fuses with the oocyte.
optionExplanations.B: Pronuclear formation occurs later and is not the primary effect of cortical granule release.
optionExplanations.C: Cleavage follows fertilization but is not the purpose of the cortical reaction.
optionExplanations.D: Trophoblast differentiation occurs during later blastocyst development.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.

questions.takeaway: Cortical reaction = block to polyspermy.
questions.recognition: Cortical granules are a post-fusion anti-polyspermy mechanism.

questions.stem: Severe DNA damage triggers mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization and cytochrome-c release. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which initiator caspase is activated downstream?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the principal initiator of mitochondrial apoptosis.
optionExplanations.C: Caspase-8 is the classic initiator of the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.D: Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase, not the primary intrinsic initiator.
optionExplanations.E: Caspase-1 is associated with inflammasome signaling.

questions.takeaway: Intrinsic apoptosis activates caspase-9; extrinsic activates caspase-8.
questions.recognition: Cytochrome c release should trigger caspase-9.

questions.stem: A prosthetic-joint infection grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci that are sensitive to novobiocin. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Device infection + coag negative + novobiocin sensitive = epidermidis.
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.
optionExplanations.B: Enterococcus is catalase negative and is identified by other biochemical features.
optionExplanations.C: This organism is catalase negative.
optionExplanations.D: S saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and classically associated with UTIs.
optionExplanations.E: S aureus is coagulase positive.

questions.takeaway: S epidermidis is the prosthetic-device staphylococcus.
questions.recognition: Novobiocin sensitivity distinguishes it from S saprophyticus.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man receives a reversible antagonist with an agonist. The agonist dose-response curve shifts to the right, but a sufficiently high agonist dose still reaches the original maximum response. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What type of antagonist was given?
questions.explanation: A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.

optionExplanations.A: Noncompetitive antagonism typically decreases maximal efficacy.
optionExplanations.B: An inverse agonist reduces constitutive receptor signaling below baseline.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.
optionExplanations.D: Irreversible blockade generally cannot be fully overcome and can reduce Emax.
optionExplanations.E: A partial agonist activates the receptor but has lower efficacy.

questions.takeaway: Competitive antagonism decreases apparent potency without decreasing maximal efficacy.
questions.recognition: If the maximum is preserved, think surmountable competitive antagonism.

questions.stem: A tumor overexpresses cyclin D1, increasing cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which molecular event most directly promotes entry into S phase?
options: Phosphorylation of RB with release of E2F
questions.hint: RB is the brake; phosphorylation releases E2F.
questions.explanation: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.

optionExplanations.A: Loss of E2F would reduce S-phase gene transcription.
optionExplanations.B: This would block rather than promote S-phase progression.
optionExplanations.C: p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and promotes arrest.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.
optionExplanations.E: Hypophosphorylated RB binds and restrains E2F.

questions.takeaway: Cyclin D/CDK4/6 → pRB → free E2F → S phase.
questions.recognition: Cyclin D questions usually converge on RB phosphorylation.

questions.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1 of every 2,500 individuals in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the mutant allele frequency q?
questions.explanation: For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.

optionExplanations.A: This is not the square root of the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.
optionExplanations.C: That would produce a substantially higher disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.D: That is q², the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.E: That would correspond to q² of 1/10,000.

questions.takeaway: Hardy-Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
questions.recognition: Take the square root before calculating carrier frequency.

questions.stem: A pesticide prevents electrons from NADH from entering the mitochondrial respiratory chain by blocking Complex I. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which compound has this effect?
questions.hint: Map each classic toxin to its ETC target.
questions.explanation: Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.
optionExplanations.B: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III.
optionExplanations.C: Cyanide inhibits Complex IV.
optionExplanations.D: 2,4-DNP uncouples oxidative phosphorylation rather than blocking Complex I.
optionExplanations.E: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase.

questions.takeaway: Rotenone = Complex I; antimycin = III; cyanide = IV; oligomycin = ATP synthase.
questions.recognition: Complex I blocker is rotenone.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a persistent firm 3-cm palpable breast mass and has never undergone breast imaging. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which initial imaging study is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.

optionExplanations.A: CT does not replace dedicated breast imaging.
optionExplanations.B: A persistent firm mass requires evaluation.
optionExplanations.C: MRI has selected indications but is not the usual first study for a palpable mass in a patient under 30.
optionExplanations.D: PET is not the first-line evaluation of a localized new breast mass.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.

questions.takeaway: Under 30 with a palpable mass → ultrasound first.
questions.recognition: Do not jump to mammography/PET in a young patient with a new mass.

questions.stem: A young woman has recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. Platelet count and PT are normal, and ristocetin-dependent activity is decreased. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.

optionExplanations.A: Glanzmann causes defective aggregation but preserves ristocetin-dependent adhesion.
optionExplanations.B: Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia, not a bleeding disorder.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.
optionExplanations.D: ITP causes thrombocytopenia, whereas this platelet count is normal.
optionExplanations.E: Hemophilia causes deep tissue bleeding and hemarthroses rather than predominantly mucosal bleeding.

questions.takeaway: vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.
questions.recognition: Menorrhagia and epistaxis point toward primary hemostasis.

questions.stem: A patient begins an HIV integrase strand-transfer inhibitor. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which stage of viral replication is directly inhibited?
options: Insertion of viral DNA into the host genome
Reverse transcription of RNA into DNA
questions.hint: Integrase does exactly what its name suggests.
questions.explanation: Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.

optionExplanations.A: Integrase inhibitors act before productive proviral transcription and budding.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.
optionExplanations.C: This is an earlier entry step.
optionExplanations.D: Protease inhibitors block maturation.
optionExplanations.E: NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription.

questions.takeaway: INSTIs block integration of viral DNA into host DNA.
questions.recognition: HIV drug-class questions often map directly to the viral life cycle.

questions.stem: A developmental defect disrupts formation of somites, producing abnormalities of vertebrae, skeletal muscle, and dermis. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which embryologic tissue was affected?
questions.hint: Somites sit beside the neural tube.
questions.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.

optionExplanations.A: Neural crest forms PNS structures, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial tissues.
optionExplanations.B: Endoderm forms many internal epithelial linings.
optionExplanations.C: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body-wall, cardiovascular, and visceral structures.
optionExplanations.D: Intermediate mesoderm contributes to kidneys, gonads, and genital ducts.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.

questions.takeaway: Paraxial mesoderm → somites.
questions.recognition: Vertebrae + muscle + dermis in one stem = somites.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell phagocytoses an extracellular bacterial protein and processes it in an endosomal compartment. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which molecule presents the peptide to helper T cells?
questions.explanation: Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: Beta-2 microglobulin is a component of MHC I and does not independently present peptide.
optionExplanations.B: CD8 is a T-cell coreceptor, not the presenting molecule.
optionExplanations.C: Fc receptors facilitate uptake/activation but are not the peptide-presenting molecule to helper T cells.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.
optionExplanations.E: MHC I usually presents endogenous intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells.

questions.takeaway: Exogenous antigen → MHC II → CD4.
questions.recognition: Phagocytosed extracellular protein is a classic MHC II setup.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman in the third trimester has sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding without uterine tenderness. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: Abruption usually causes painful bleeding and a tender, firm uterus.
optionExplanations.B: Molar pregnancy typically presents earlier with abnormal trophoblastic findings.
optionExplanations.C: Accreta causes abnormal adherence and postpartum hemorrhage rather than classic painless antepartum bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: This usually causes fever and uterine tenderness.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Previa is painless; abruption is painful.
questions.recognition: The pain distinction is the fastest way to separate previa from abruption.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has a hormone that binds a Gs-coupled receptor on target cells. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which intracellular change occurs first downstream of the activated G alpha subunit?
options: Activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased cAMP
Activation of phospholipase C and increased IP3/DAG
Activation of receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation
questions.explanation: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.

optionExplanations.A: JAK/STAT is used by cytokine receptors rather than classical Gs-coupled GPCRs.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.
optionExplanations.C: This is the classic Gq pathway.
optionExplanations.D: That belongs to RTK signaling, not Gs GPCR signaling.
optionExplanations.E: This is the classic Gi effect.

questions.takeaway: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.
questions.recognition: The letter “s” in Gs can be remembered as “stimulates” adenylyl cyclase.

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, beta-oxidation raises mitochondrial acetyl-CoA. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is directly activated by acetyl-CoA?
questions.hint: High acetyl-CoA tells the liver to spare pyruvate for glucose production.
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.
optionExplanations.B: PFK-1 controls glycolysis and is not activated by acetyl-CoA.
optionExplanations.C: Hexokinase is not directly activated by acetyl-CoA.
optionExplanations.D: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme and is inhibited during hepatic fasting.
optionExplanations.E: This enzyme is regulated mainly by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rather than direct acetyl-CoA activation.

questions.takeaway: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase.
questions.recognition: Fasting + acetyl-CoA + gluconeogenesis = pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: A bacterial pneumonia is treated with a beta-lactam antibiotic that covalently binds penicillin-binding proteins. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which process is directly inhibited?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: Rifamycins inhibit bacterial RNA polymerase.
optionExplanations.B: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines target the 30S subunit.
optionExplanations.C: Sulfonamides and trimethoprim inhibit folate pathways.
optionExplanations.D: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.

questions.takeaway: Beta-lactams inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking.
questions.recognition: Cell-wall question + PBP should be automatic.

questions.stem: A woman has endometrial cancer and a strong family history of early-onset colorectal cancer. Her tumor shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 expression. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which hereditary syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.

optionExplanations.A: FAP is caused by APC mutations and usually causes hundreds to thousands of adenomas.
optionExplanations.B: This is caused by RB1 loss.
optionExplanations.C: MEN2 is due to activating RET mutations.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.
optionExplanations.E: Li-Fraumeni is due to germline TP53 mutations and a different tumor spectrum.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome is a mismatch-repair cancer syndrome.
questions.recognition: MSH2/MSH6 loss is a strong clue for Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer is still receiving chemotherapy but has severe pain, nausea, anxiety, and difficulty discussing future goals. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which statement about palliative care is most accurate?
options: It is appropriate only after cancer therapy stops
It requires a prognosis under 6 months
It can be provided concurrently with disease-directed therapy
It is limited to opioid management
questions.hint: Do not equate palliative care with hospice.
questions.explanation: Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Palliative care can begin early and coexist with treatment.
optionExplanations.B: That criterion is more characteristic of hospice eligibility.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.
optionExplanations.D: Hospice is a narrower end-of-life model within the broader palliative approach.
optionExplanations.E: Palliative care addresses symptoms, communication, psychosocial support, and goals of care.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care can be concurrent with active treatment.
questions.recognition: If the stem says “still receiving treatment,” palliative care can still be appropriate.

questions.stem: A patient has mucosal bleeding. Platelet count is normal. Aggregation is impaired with most agonists, but ristocetin response is preserved. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which receptor is defective?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.

optionExplanations.A: P2Y12 participates in ADP-mediated platelet activation but does not produce the classic pattern described.
optionExplanations.B: Thrombomodulin participates in the protein C anticoagulant pathway.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.
optionExplanations.D: GpIb deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.E: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A with deep tissue bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Glanzmann = GpIIb/IIIa aggregation defect.
questions.recognition: Differentiate Glanzmann from Bernard-Soulier using ristocetin.

questions.stem: A child has extreme photosensitivity and develops multiple skin cancers on sun-exposed areas. Cells cannot appropriately remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
optionExplanations.B: HR repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous template.
optionExplanations.C: MMR corrects replication mismatches and insertion-deletion loops.
optionExplanations.D: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks without a homologous template.
optionExplanations.E: BER repairs small, non-helix-distorting base lesions.

questions.takeaway: NER removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions.
questions.recognition: UV sensitivity plus early skin cancers should trigger xeroderma pigmentosum and NER.

questions.stem: A patient receives a foreign protein. One week later, fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and low complement develop. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.hint: Immune complexes + low complement = Type III.
questions.explanation: Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.

optionExplanations.A: Loss of tolerance may cause autoimmunity but does not describe this immune-complex effector mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: Type IV is T-cell mediated.
optionExplanations.C: Type II targets fixed cell-surface/tissue antigens.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.
optionExplanations.E: Type I is immediate and IgE mediated.

questions.takeaway: Type III = circulating immune-complex deposition.
questions.recognition: Fever + rash + arthralgia after foreign protein is serum sickness.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient has an automated platelet count of 35,000/µL, but the peripheral smear shows numerous platelet clumps. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the platelet count with a fresh specimen and evaluate for laboratory artifact
questions.hint: Always inspect the smear before treating the number.
questions.explanation: Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.

optionExplanations.A: An asymptomatic patient with obvious clumping may not truly be thrombocytopenic.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.
optionExplanations.C: Plasma exchange is used in TTP, which would require a different clinical picture.
optionExplanations.D: This is unnecessarily invasive before excluding pseudothrombocytopenia.
optionExplanations.E: Do not diagnose immune thrombocytopenia before confirming that the low count is real.

questions.takeaway: Platelet clumping can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.recognition: Asymptomatic + clumps = pseudothrombocytopenia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man receives a drug by continuous IV infusion. Renal function improves and the drug clearance doubles while the desired steady-state concentration remains unchanged. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What dosing change is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.
optionExplanations.B: Lowering the rate would further reduce steady-state exposure.
optionExplanations.C: Loading dose depends mainly on volume of distribution and target concentration, not clearance.
optionExplanations.D: Volume of distribution is not a dosing adjustment.
optionExplanations.E: Higher clearance lowers steady-state concentration unless dosing rate is increased.

questions.takeaway: Maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.
questions.recognition: When clearance changes, maintenance dosing changes; loading dose is tied to Vd.

questions.stem: A child has impaired phagocytosis of encapsulated bacteria because the organisms are not efficiently coated for complement-receptor recognition. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which complement component normally performs this function?
questions.explanation: C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: C9 participates in the membrane attack complex.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.
optionExplanations.C: C5a is a potent chemotactic and inflammatory mediator.
optionExplanations.D: C1 inhibitor regulates complement/contact activation rather than opsonizing microbes.
optionExplanations.E: C3a is mainly an anaphylatoxin.

questions.takeaway: C3b coats; C3a/C5a inflame; C5b-9 punches holes.
questions.recognition: Encapsulated organism + complement receptor = C3b.

questions.stem: A cancer-screening program detects tumors several years earlier. Five-year survival after diagnosis increases, but cancer-specific mortality is unchanged. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which bias best explains the apparent benefit?
questions.hint: Earlier diagnosis without later death = lead-time bias.
questions.explanation: Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.

optionExplanations.A: Recall bias affects remembered exposures.
optionExplanations.B: Selection bias concerns who enters or remains in a study.
optionExplanations.C: Observer bias arises from measurement influenced by expectations.
optionExplanations.D: Length-time bias preferentially detects slower-growing disease.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.

questions.takeaway: Lead-time bias inflates post-diagnosis survival without improving mortality.
questions.recognition: Always compare survival to disease-specific mortality in screening questions.

questions.stem: A patient with candidemia receives micafungin. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which fungal structure is most directly disrupted?
options: Ergosterol in the membrane through pore formation
Beta-1,3-D-glucan component of the fungal cell wall
questions.explanation: Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.

optionExplanations.A: Flucytosine metabolites interfere with nucleic-acid synthesis, not beta-glucan.
optionExplanations.B: Azoles inhibit this enzyme and reduce ergosterol synthesis.
optionExplanations.C: Polyenes bind ergosterol and form pores.
optionExplanations.D: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.

questions.takeaway: Micafungin inhibits beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis.
questions.recognition: Candida + micafungin should trigger echinocandin cell-wall inhibition.

questions.stem: An older adult has large tense blisters. Biopsy shows the entire epidermis separating from the underlying basement membrane while epidermal cells remain attached to one another. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which structure is targeted?
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.
optionExplanations.B: Adherens junctions link actin cytoskeletons between cells.
optionExplanations.C: Tight junctions regulate paracellular permeability.
optionExplanations.D: Desmosomal disruption produces intraepidermal acantholysis and flaccid blisters.
optionExplanations.E: Gap junctions mediate cell communication.

questions.takeaway: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes.
questions.recognition: Flaccid = desmosomes; tense = hemidesmosomes.

questions.stem: A breast-fed infant develops vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and cataracts. Urine contains a reducing sugar but the glucose dipstick is negative. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Milk exposure + cataracts + liver disease = classic galactosemia.
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.

optionExplanations.A: This causes von Gierke disease rather than a milk-triggered galactose syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign fructosuria.
optionExplanations.C: Galactokinase deficiency is milder and mainly causes cataracts without severe hepatic disease.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.
optionExplanations.E: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance after fruit/sucrose exposure.

questions.takeaway: Classic galactosemia = GALT deficiency.
questions.recognition: If cataracts are accompanied by severe systemic toxicity, distinguish GALT deficiency from isolated galactokinase deficiency.

questions.stem: A sperm penetrates the zona pellucida and fuses with the oocyte membrane. Cortical granules are released immediately afterward. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What is the main purpose of the cortical reaction?
questions.hint: One sperm in; lock the door.
questions.explanation: The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.

optionExplanations.A: Pronuclear formation occurs later and is not the primary effect of cortical granule release.
optionExplanations.B: Capacitation occurs before the sperm reaches and fuses with the oocyte.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.
optionExplanations.D: Cleavage follows fertilization but is not the purpose of the cortical reaction.
optionExplanations.E: Trophoblast differentiation occurs during later blastocyst development.

questions.takeaway: Cortical reaction = block to polyspermy.
questions.recognition: Cortical granules are a post-fusion anti-polyspermy mechanism.

questions.stem: Severe DNA damage triggers mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization and cytochrome-c release. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which initiator caspase is activated downstream?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.

optionExplanations.A: This is not the principal initiator of mitochondrial apoptosis.
optionExplanations.B: Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase, not the primary intrinsic initiator.
optionExplanations.C: Caspase-8 is the classic initiator of the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.
optionExplanations.E: Caspase-1 is associated with inflammasome signaling.

questions.takeaway: Intrinsic apoptosis activates caspase-9; extrinsic activates caspase-8.
questions.recognition: Cytochrome c release should trigger caspase-9.

questions.stem: A young child has severe microcytic anemia, marrow expansion, skeletal changes, hepatosplenomegaly, and transfusion dependence. Hemoglobin analysis shows very high HbF and almost no HbA. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: High HbF + absent HbA + severe childhood disease = beta-thal major.
questions.explanation: Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.

optionExplanations.A: Alpha trait is generally mild microcytosis.
optionExplanations.B: Iron deficiency does not produce this hemoglobin pattern or marrow-expansion syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.
optionExplanations.D: HbC trait is generally mild.
optionExplanations.E: Sickle trait has HbA greater than HbS and is usually asymptomatic.

questions.takeaway: Beta-thalassemia major causes severe ineffective erythropoiesis.
questions.recognition: Think of globin composition, not just microcytosis.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain says, “My spine must be getting destroyed. It will only get worse, and there is nothing I can do.” The patient spends hours ruminating about the pain. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which psychological construct is most strongly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.

optionExplanations.A: Acceptance is adaptive willingness to experience pain while functioning.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.
optionExplanations.C: Values-based action involves pursuing meaningful activities despite symptoms.
optionExplanations.D: Self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function despite pain.
optionExplanations.E: Pacing is structured activity management.

questions.takeaway: Catastrophizing = rumination + magnification + helplessness.
questions.recognition: “It is terrible and I cannot cope” is the core cognitive pattern.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell phagocytoses an extracellular bacterial protein and processes it in an endosomal compartment. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which molecule presents the peptide to helper T cells?
questions.explanation: Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: Fc receptors facilitate uptake/activation but are not the peptide-presenting molecule to helper T cells.
optionExplanations.B: CD8 is a T-cell coreceptor, not the presenting molecule.
optionExplanations.C: MHC I usually presents endogenous intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells.
optionExplanations.D: Beta-2 microglobulin is a component of MHC I and does not independently present peptide.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.

questions.takeaway: Exogenous antigen → MHC II → CD4.
questions.recognition: Phagocytosed extracellular protein is a classic MHC II setup.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a persistent firm 3-cm palpable breast mass and has never undergone breast imaging. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which initial imaging study is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.

optionExplanations.A: PET is not the first-line evaluation of a localized new breast mass.
optionExplanations.B: A persistent firm mass requires evaluation.
optionExplanations.C: CT does not replace dedicated breast imaging.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.
optionExplanations.E: MRI has selected indications but is not the usual first study for a palpable mass in a patient under 30.

questions.takeaway: Under 30 with a palpable mass → ultrasound first.
questions.recognition: Do not jump to mammography/PET in a young patient with a new mass.

questions.stem: A prosthetic-joint infection grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci that are sensitive to novobiocin. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Device infection + coag negative + novobiocin sensitive = epidermidis.
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.

optionExplanations.A: S saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and classically associated with UTIs.
optionExplanations.B: S aureus is coagulase positive.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.
optionExplanations.D: Enterococcus is catalase negative and is identified by other biochemical features.
optionExplanations.E: This organism is catalase negative.

questions.takeaway: S epidermidis is the prosthetic-device staphylococcus.
questions.recognition: Novobiocin sensitivity distinguishes it from S saprophyticus.

questions.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1 of every 2,500 individuals in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the mutant allele frequency q?
questions.explanation: For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.

optionExplanations.A: That is q², the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.
optionExplanations.C: This is not the square root of the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.D: That would produce a substantially higher disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.E: That would correspond to q² of 1/10,000.

questions.takeaway: Hardy-Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
questions.recognition: Take the square root before calculating carrier frequency.

questions.stem: A young woman has recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. Platelet count and PT are normal, and ristocetin-dependent activity is decreased. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.
optionExplanations.B: Glanzmann causes defective aggregation but preserves ristocetin-dependent adhesion.
optionExplanations.C: Hemophilia causes deep tissue bleeding and hemarthroses rather than predominantly mucosal bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: ITP causes thrombocytopenia, whereas this platelet count is normal.
optionExplanations.E: Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia, not a bleeding disorder.

questions.takeaway: vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.
questions.recognition: Menorrhagia and epistaxis point toward primary hemostasis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman receives a reversible antagonist with an agonist. The agonist dose-response curve shifts to the right, but a sufficiently high agonist dose still reaches the original maximum response. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What type of antagonist was given?
questions.explanation: A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.

optionExplanations.A: Irreversible blockade generally cannot be fully overcome and can reduce Emax.
optionExplanations.B: Noncompetitive antagonism typically decreases maximal efficacy.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.
optionExplanations.D: An inverse agonist reduces constitutive receptor signaling below baseline.
optionExplanations.E: A partial agonist activates the receptor but has lower efficacy.

questions.takeaway: Competitive antagonism decreases apparent potency without decreasing maximal efficacy.
questions.recognition: If the maximum is preserved, think surmountable competitive antagonism.

questions.stem: A pesticide prevents electrons from NADH from entering the mitochondrial respiratory chain by blocking Complex I. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which compound has this effect?
questions.hint: Map each classic toxin to its ETC target.
questions.explanation: Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.

optionExplanations.A: Cyanide inhibits Complex IV.
optionExplanations.B: 2,4-DNP uncouples oxidative phosphorylation rather than blocking Complex I.
optionExplanations.C: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.
optionExplanations.E: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III.

questions.takeaway: Rotenone = Complex I; antimycin = III; cyanide = IV; oligomycin = ATP synthase.
questions.recognition: Complex I blocker is rotenone.

questions.stem: A developmental defect disrupts formation of somites, producing abnormalities of vertebrae, skeletal muscle, and dermis. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which embryologic tissue was affected?
questions.hint: Somites sit beside the neural tube.
questions.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.

optionExplanations.A: Neural crest forms PNS structures, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial tissues.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.
optionExplanations.C: Endoderm forms many internal epithelial linings.
optionExplanations.D: Intermediate mesoderm contributes to kidneys, gonads, and genital ducts.
optionExplanations.E: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body-wall, cardiovascular, and visceral structures.

questions.takeaway: Paraxial mesoderm → somites.
questions.recognition: Vertebrae + muscle + dermis in one stem = somites.

questions.stem: A patient begins an HIV integrase strand-transfer inhibitor. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which stage of viral replication is directly inhibited?
options: Insertion of viral DNA into the host genome
Reverse transcription of RNA into DNA
questions.hint: Integrase does exactly what its name suggests.
questions.explanation: Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.
optionExplanations.B: NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription.
optionExplanations.C: Integrase inhibitors act before productive proviral transcription and budding.
optionExplanations.D: Protease inhibitors block maturation.
optionExplanations.E: This is an earlier entry step.

questions.takeaway: INSTIs block integration of viral DNA into host DNA.
questions.recognition: HIV drug-class questions often map directly to the viral life cycle.

questions.stem: A tumor overexpresses cyclin D1, increasing cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which molecular event most directly promotes entry into S phase?
options: Phosphorylation of RB with release of E2F
questions.hint: RB is the brake; phosphorylation releases E2F.
questions.explanation: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.

optionExplanations.A: Hypophosphorylated RB binds and restrains E2F.
optionExplanations.B: p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and promotes arrest.
optionExplanations.C: This would block rather than promote S-phase progression.
optionExplanations.D: Loss of E2F would reduce S-phase gene transcription.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.

questions.takeaway: Cyclin D/CDK4/6 → pRB → free E2F → S phase.
questions.recognition: Cyclin D questions usually converge on RB phosphorylation.

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, beta-oxidation raises mitochondrial acetyl-CoA. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme is directly activated by acetyl-CoA?
questions.hint: High acetyl-CoA tells the liver to spare pyruvate for glucose production.
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.

optionExplanations.A: This enzyme is regulated mainly by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rather than direct acetyl-CoA activation.
optionExplanations.B: PFK-1 controls glycolysis and is not activated by acetyl-CoA.
optionExplanations.C: Hexokinase is not directly activated by acetyl-CoA.
optionExplanations.D: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme and is inhibited during hepatic fasting.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.

questions.takeaway: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase.
questions.recognition: Fasting + acetyl-CoA + gluconeogenesis = pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: A woman has endometrial cancer and a strong family history of early-onset colorectal cancer. Her tumor shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 expression. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which hereditary syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.

optionExplanations.A: MEN2 is due to activating RET mutations.
optionExplanations.B: FAP is caused by APC mutations and usually causes hundreds to thousands of adenomas.
optionExplanations.C: This is caused by RB1 loss.
