optionExplanations.D: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.
optionExplanations.E: Li-Fraumeni is due to germline TP53 mutations and a different tumor spectrum.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome is a mismatch-repair cancer syndrome.
questions.recognition: MSH2/MSH6 loss is a strong clue for Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman in the third trimester has sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding without uterine tenderness. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: This usually causes fever and uterine tenderness.
optionExplanations.B: Accreta causes abnormal adherence and postpartum hemorrhage rather than classic painless antepartum bleeding.
optionExplanations.C: Molar pregnancy typically presents earlier with abnormal trophoblastic findings.
optionExplanations.D: Abruption usually causes painful bleeding and a tender, firm uterus.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Previa is painless; abruption is painful.
questions.recognition: The pain distinction is the fastest way to separate previa from abruption.

questions.stem: A child has extreme photosensitivity and develops multiple skin cancers on sun-exposed areas. Cells cannot appropriately remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

optionExplanations.A: MMR corrects replication mismatches and insertion-deletion loops.
optionExplanations.B: BER repairs small, non-helix-distorting base lesions.
optionExplanations.C: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks without a homologous template.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
optionExplanations.E: HR repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous template.

questions.takeaway: NER removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions.
questions.recognition: UV sensitivity plus early skin cancers should trigger xeroderma pigmentosum and NER.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man has a hormone that binds a Gs-coupled receptor on target cells. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which intracellular change occurs first downstream of the activated G alpha subunit?
options: Activation of phospholipase C and increased IP3/DAG
Activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased cAMP
Activation of receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation
questions.explanation: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.

optionExplanations.A: This is the classic Gq pathway.
optionExplanations.B: This is the classic Gi effect.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.
optionExplanations.D: JAK/STAT is used by cytokine receptors rather than classical Gs-coupled GPCRs.
optionExplanations.E: That belongs to RTK signaling, not Gs GPCR signaling.

questions.takeaway: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.
questions.recognition: The letter “s” in Gs can be remembered as “stimulates” adenylyl cyclase.

questions.stem: A patient receives a foreign protein. One week later, fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and low complement develop. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.hint: Immune complexes + low complement = Type III.
questions.explanation: Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.

optionExplanations.A: Type I is immediate and IgE mediated.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.
optionExplanations.C: Type II targets fixed cell-surface/tissue antigens.
optionExplanations.D: Type IV is T-cell mediated.
optionExplanations.E: Loss of tolerance may cause autoimmunity but does not describe this immune-complex effector mechanism.

questions.takeaway: Type III = circulating immune-complex deposition.
questions.recognition: Fever + rash + arthralgia after foreign protein is serum sickness.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer is still receiving chemotherapy but has severe pain, nausea, anxiety, and difficulty discussing future goals. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which statement about palliative care is most accurate?
options: It can be provided concurrently with disease-directed therapy
It is limited to opioid management
It is appropriate only after cancer therapy stops
It requires a prognosis under 6 months
questions.hint: Do not equate palliative care with hospice.
questions.explanation: Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.
optionExplanations.B: Hospice is a narrower end-of-life model within the broader palliative approach.
optionExplanations.C: Palliative care addresses symptoms, communication, psychosocial support, and goals of care.
optionExplanations.D: Palliative care can begin early and coexist with treatment.
optionExplanations.E: That criterion is more characteristic of hospice eligibility.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care can be concurrent with active treatment.
questions.recognition: If the stem says “still receiving treatment,” palliative care can still be appropriate.

questions.stem: A bacterial pneumonia is treated with a beta-lactam antibiotic that covalently binds penicillin-binding proteins. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which process is directly inhibited?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines target the 30S subunit.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.
optionExplanations.C: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase.
optionExplanations.D: Rifamycins inhibit bacterial RNA polymerase.
optionExplanations.E: Sulfonamides and trimethoprim inhibit folate pathways.

questions.takeaway: Beta-lactams inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking.
questions.recognition: Cell-wall question + PBP should be automatic.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient has an automated platelet count of 35,000/µL, but the peripheral smear shows numerous platelet clumps. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the platelet count with a fresh specimen and evaluate for laboratory artifact
questions.hint: Always inspect the smear before treating the number.
questions.explanation: Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.

optionExplanations.A: Plasma exchange is used in TTP, which would require a different clinical picture.
optionExplanations.B: This is unnecessarily invasive before excluding pseudothrombocytopenia.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.
optionExplanations.D: An asymptomatic patient with obvious clumping may not truly be thrombocytopenic.
optionExplanations.E: Do not diagnose immune thrombocytopenia before confirming that the low count is real.

questions.takeaway: Platelet clumping can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.recognition: Asymptomatic + clumps = pseudothrombocytopenia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A patient has mucosal bleeding. Platelet count is normal. Aggregation is impaired with most agonists, but ristocetin response is preserved. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which receptor is defective?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.
optionExplanations.B: P2Y12 participates in ADP-mediated platelet activation but does not produce the classic pattern described.
optionExplanations.C: GpIb deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.D: Thrombomodulin participates in the protein C anticoagulant pathway.
optionExplanations.E: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A with deep tissue bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Glanzmann = GpIIb/IIIa aggregation defect.
questions.recognition: Differentiate Glanzmann from Bernard-Soulier using ristocetin.

questions.stem: A patient has flaccid skin blisters and oral erosions. Biopsy shows acantholysis within the epidermis. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which structure is targeted by autoantibodies?
questions.explanation: Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins in desmosomes, causing loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion and flaccid intraepidermal blisters.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by autoantibodies against desmogleins in desmosomes, causing loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion and flaccid intraepidermal blisters.
optionExplanations.B: Connexins form gap junctions.
optionExplanations.C: Hemidesmosomal targets are more relevant to bullous pemphigoid.
optionExplanations.D: Claudins are tight-junction proteins.
optionExplanations.E: Type IV collagen is a basement-membrane component and does not explain intraepidermal acantholysis.

questions.takeaway: Pemphigus targets desmogleins.
questions.recognition: Flaccid blisters plus mucosal involvement should make you think pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.stem: An infant develops vomiting, sweating, profound hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly shortly after fruit juice is introduced. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Symptoms begin when fructose/sucrose enters the diet.
questions.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign essential fructosuria.
optionExplanations.B: Galactokinase deficiency primarily causes cataracts.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.D: This causes von Gierke disease and is not specifically triggered by fructose introduction.
optionExplanations.E: GALT deficiency causes classic galactosemia after milk exposure.

questions.takeaway: Hereditary fructose intolerance = aldolase B deficiency.
questions.recognition: Fruit introduction + hypoglycemia + liver dysfunction is the classic pattern.

questions.stem: A child with chronic hemolytic anemia has deletion of three alpha-globin genes. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which abnormal hemoglobin is expected?
options: Hb Barts composed of gamma4 tetramers
questions.explanation: Three alpha-globin gene deletions cause HbH disease. In adults, excess beta chains form beta4 tetramers called HbH.

optionExplanations.A: HbA2 is elevated in beta-thalassemia trait but is not dominant here.
optionExplanations.B: Hb Barts is most severe in four-gene alpha deletion during fetal life.
optionExplanations.C: HbS results from a beta-globin missense mutation.
optionExplanations.D: HbC is a structural beta-chain variant.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Three alpha-globin gene deletions cause HbH disease. In adults, excess beta chains form beta4 tetramers called HbH.

questions.takeaway: HbH = beta4 from three alpha-gene deletions.
questions.recognition: Four alpha deletions give gamma4 Hb Barts; three give beta4 HbH.

questions.stem: A healthy sperm reaches the secondary oocyte under normal physiologic conditions. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Where does fertilization most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.

optionExplanations.A: The cervix is part of the sperm’s route but not the usual fertilization site.
optionExplanations.B: The ampulla, not the isthmus, is the most common site.
optionExplanations.C: The oocyte is released from the ovary before fertilization.
optionExplanations.D: The blastocyst later implants in the uterus; fertilization usually occurs before arrival there.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.

questions.takeaway: Fertilization = ampulla; implantation = endometrium.
questions.recognition: Ampulla is the classic normal fertilization site.

questions.stem: A hypoxic cell develops ATP depletion, ion-pump failure, and marked intracellular calcium accumulation. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme activities most directly worsen structural injury?
options: Glycogen synthase and protein kinase A
questions.hint: High intracellular calcium turns on destructive enzymes.
questions.explanation: Elevated cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes and proteases that degrade cytoskeletal and structural proteins. Calcium also worsens mitochondrial dysfunction.

optionExplanations.A: These ATP-dependent pumps fail rather than become destructive effectors.
optionExplanations.B: These do not explain calcium-mediated membrane and cytoskeletal destruction.
optionExplanations.C: These are not the main calcium-activated destructive enzymes in acute injury.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Elevated cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes and proteases that degrade cytoskeletal and structural proteins. Calcium also worsens mitochondrial dysfunction.
optionExplanations.E: These are not acute effectors of calcium-mediated necrotic injury.

questions.takeaway: Calcium activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases.
questions.recognition: In ischemic injury, calcium is dangerous because it activates degradative enzymes.

questions.stem: A patient with an anaerobic intra-abdominal infection receives metronidazole. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which mechanism best describes its antimicrobial effect?
options: Reactive metabolites damage microbial DNA and cause strand breaks
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is reduced within susceptible anaerobic organisms and generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA, causing strand breaks.

optionExplanations.A: That is a beta-lactam mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: Trimethoprim inhibits DHFR.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Metronidazole is reduced within susceptible anaerobic organisms and generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA, causing strand breaks.
optionExplanations.D: This is not metronidazole’s mechanism.
optionExplanations.E: This is an antifungal mechanism.

questions.takeaway: Metronidazole creates toxic radicals that damage DNA.
questions.recognition: Think anaerobes/protozoa and DNA strand breaks.

questions.stem: A treatment truly reduces recurrence, but an underpowered study reports no statistically significant difference from placebo. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which quantity is the probability of making this error?
questions.explanation: Failing to detect a true effect is a Type II error. The probability of a Type II error is beta, and statistical power equals 1 − beta.

optionExplanations.A: Alpha is the probability of a Type I false-positive error.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Failing to detect a true effect is a Type II error. The probability of a Type II error is beta, and statistical power equals 1 − beta.
optionExplanations.C: Sensitivity is a diagnostic-test property.
optionExplanations.D: This is not the probability of a Type II error.
optionExplanations.E: Power is 1 − beta and represents the probability of detecting a true effect.

questions.takeaway: Beta is the Type II error probability; power = 1 − beta.
questions.recognition: Underpowered + real difference missed = beta.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is given an oral solute that crosses an epithelial membrane through a specific carrier without direct ATP hydrolysis. Transport rises with concentration and then reaches a plateau. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which transport mechanism best fits these findings?
questions.hint: The clue is “down gradient + carrier + saturation + no ATP.”
questions.explanation: Facilitated diffusion uses a finite number of carrier proteins to move solute down its electrochemical gradient. Because carrier number is limited, the process is saturable even though ATP is not directly consumed.

optionExplanations.A: Endocytosis uses vesicles rather than a saturable membrane carrier for small solutes.
optionExplanations.B: Secondary active transport couples movement to another ion gradient and can move a solute uphill.
optionExplanations.C: Simple diffusion is not carrier-saturable.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Facilitated diffusion uses a finite number of carrier proteins to move solute down its electrochemical gradient. Because carrier number is limited, the process is saturable even though ATP is not directly consumed.
optionExplanations.E: Primary active transport directly hydrolyzes ATP.

questions.takeaway: Facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated, passive, and saturable.
questions.recognition: A plateau in transport rate strongly suggests carrier saturation.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic pain says, “I may not eliminate the pain, but I am willing to experience some discomfort so I can keep doing what matters to me.”. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which construct is best demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Pain acceptance is willingness to experience pain without allowing it to control participation in valued activities.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pain acceptance is willingness to experience pain without allowing it to control participation in valued activities.
optionExplanations.B: Hypervigilance is excessive attention to bodily sensations.
optionExplanations.C: Somatization does not describe this adaptive willingness to function despite discomfort.
optionExplanations.D: Catastrophizing focuses on worst-case interpretations and helplessness.
optionExplanations.E: Fear avoidance leads patients to restrict activity due to concern about pain or injury.

questions.takeaway: Acceptance means making room for pain while pursuing meaningful function.
questions.recognition: The key is not giving up; it is acting according to values despite pain.

questions.stem: A child has normal or elevated IgM but profoundly reduced IgG, IgA, and IgE. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which defect most likely prevents class switching?
questions.hint: IgM high, other isotypes low = class-switch failure.
questions.explanation: T-dependent class switching requires CD40 on B cells interacting with CD40L on activated helper T cells. CD40L deficiency produces hyper-IgM syndrome.

optionExplanations.A: MPO is a neutrophil microbicidal enzyme.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. T-dependent class switching requires CD40 on B cells interacting with CD40L on activated helper T cells. CD40L deficiency produces hyper-IgM syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: Factor H regulates complement rather than immunoglobulin switching.
optionExplanations.D: C5 deficiency predisposes to Neisseria.
optionExplanations.E: TAP deficiency impairs MHC I antigen presentation.

questions.takeaway: CD40-CD40L signaling is required for T-dependent class switching.
questions.recognition: Hyper-IgM is the classic CD40L clue.

questions.stem: A respiratory epithelial cell is infected with an intracellular virus. Viral proteins are synthesized in the cytosol. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which antigen-presentation pathway activates cytotoxic T cells?
options: Fc receptor binding → direct CD8 activation
Complement opsonization → MHC class II only
B-cell receptor uptake → MHC class I
Proteasome degradation → TAP transport into ER → MHC class I
questions.explanation: Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: CD8 T cells recognize peptide-MHC I, not Fc receptor-bound antigen.
optionExplanations.B: Complement can enhance uptake but does not define the endogenous MHC I pathway.
optionExplanations.C: BCR-mediated uptake generally feeds MHC II presentation.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Endogenous cytosolic proteins are degraded by proteasomes. Peptides enter the ER via TAP, load onto MHC class I, and are recognized by CD8 T cells.
optionExplanations.E: This is the classic exogenous-antigen pathway for CD4 T cells.

questions.takeaway: Endogenous antigen → proteasome/TAP/MHC I → CD8.
questions.recognition: Virus made inside a nucleated cell should trigger MHC I.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced cancer experiences profound spiritual and existential distress about meaning, mortality, and separation from a faith community. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which team member is best suited to address this concern?
questions.hint: Match spiritual distress with spiritual care.
questions.explanation: Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.

optionExplanations.A: This is a technical radiation-therapy role.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Pastoral or spiritual-care clinicians are trained to address existential, religious, spiritual, and meaning-related distress within serious illness.
optionExplanations.C: Pathologists establish diagnoses from tissues and laboratory specimens.
optionExplanations.D: Physical therapy targets mobility, strength, and deconditioning.
optionExplanations.E: A dietitian focuses on nutrition and intake.

questions.takeaway: Pastoral care addresses existential and spiritual concerns.
questions.recognition: Do not send a meaning-of-life concern to a purely technical service.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man has kidney failure while taking a drug cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. The volume of distribution is unchanged. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which pharmacokinetic parameter will increase?
questions.explanation: Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.

optionExplanations.A: Renal failure decreases clearance.
optionExplanations.B: Affinity is pharmacodynamic and does not change because of renal failure.
optionExplanations.C: The elimination rate constant falls when clearance falls relative to Vd.
optionExplanations.D: Renal clearance does not inherently raise absorption or bioavailability.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Elimination half-life is proportional to Vd/clearance. When clearance falls and Vd is unchanged, the drug remains in the body longer and half-life increases.

questions.takeaway: Lower clearance means longer half-life when Vd is constant.
questions.recognition: Renal failure + renally cleared drug should make you think accumulation and prolonged half-life.

questions.stem: During gastrulation, cells migrate through the primitive streak to create the embryo proper. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which cell population gives rise to ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm?
questions.hint: The embryo proper comes from the upper bilaminar-disc layer.
questions.explanation: All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.

optionExplanations.A: This invasive trophoblastic layer participates in implantation and placental development.
optionExplanations.B: This is a trophoblastic placental layer.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast cells during gastrulation.
optionExplanations.D: This supports extraembryonic structures rather than generating all three germ layers of the embryo proper.
optionExplanations.E: The hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic endoderm.

questions.takeaway: Epiblast gives rise to all three germ layers.
questions.recognition: Primitive streak + all germ layers = epiblast.

questions.stem: A patient with acyclovir-resistant HSV has a viral strain lacking functional thymidine kinase. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which antiviral is the best alternative?
questions.hint: No viral TK? Choose a drug that does not need it.
questions.explanation: Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Foscarnet directly inhibits viral DNA polymerase and does not require phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, making it useful for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV.
optionExplanations.B: Interferon does not bypass the thymidine-kinase activation problem as directly as foscarnet.
optionExplanations.C: Zidovudine is an NRTI used for HIV.
optionExplanations.D: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor for influenza.
optionExplanations.E: Ribavirin is used in selected viral infections but is not the standard rescue agent for TK-deficient HSV.

questions.takeaway: Foscarnet bypasses thymidine-kinase activation.
questions.recognition: TK-deficient HSV is the classic foscarnet scenario.

questions.stem: An older adult has anemia, renal dysfunction, hypercalcemia, back pain, multiple lytic lesions, and a monoclonal protein spike. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which cell type is undergoing malignant proliferation?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Multiple myeloma is a clonal plasma-cell neoplasm. The CRAB features are hyperCalcemia, Renal dysfunction, Anemia, and Bone lesions.
optionExplanations.B: These are seen in T-ALL/LBL.
optionExplanations.C: These define classical Hodgkin lymphoma.
optionExplanations.D: These are myeloid cells and do not explain a monoclonal immunoglobulin syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Monocytes are not the malignant population responsible for CRAB findings.

questions.takeaway: Multiple myeloma is a plasma-cell malignancy.
questions.recognition: Punched-out/lytic bone lesions plus monoclonal protein are classic.

questions.stem: A patient has severe hypertriglyceridemia, eruptive xanthomas, and recurrent pancreatitis. Lipoprotein lipase is structurally normal, but its required apolipoprotein activator is absent. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which apolipoprotein is deficient?
questions.explanation: ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II deficiency therefore causes severe chylomicronemia and pancreatitis.

optionExplanations.A: ApoA-I activates LCAT and is central to HDL metabolism.
optionExplanations.B: ApoE mediates hepatic uptake of remnant particles.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. ApoC-II activates lipoprotein lipase, which hydrolyzes triglycerides in chylomicrons and VLDL. ApoC-II deficiency therefore causes severe chylomicronemia and pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.D: ApoB-48 is structural for chylomicrons.
optionExplanations.E: ApoB-100 is structural for VLDL/LDL and binds the LDL receptor.

questions.takeaway: ApoC-II activates LPL.
questions.recognition: Severe triglycerides + pancreatitis can be LPL deficiency or ApoC-II deficiency.

questions.stem: An affected father has an X-linked recessive disorder. The mother is not a carrier. Which outcome is expected for their children?
options: All sons inherit the mutant X chromosome
All daughters inherit the mutant X chromosome
questions.hint: Remember: fathers give X to daughters and Y to sons.
questions.explanation: A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.

optionExplanations.A: Sons receive the father’s Y chromosome.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A father transmits his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y chromosome to every son. Thus all daughters inherit the mutant X, while no sons inherit it from him.
optionExplanations.C: No son receives the father’s X chromosome.
optionExplanations.D: Sons do not inherit the paternal X chromosome.
optionExplanations.E: Daughters inherit the paternal mutant X but also a normal maternal X, so they are generally carriers.

questions.takeaway: X-linked disorders show no father-to-son transmission.
questions.recognition: If the affected parent is the father, trace his X only into daughters.

questions.stem: A sexually active young woman has cystitis. Culture grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci that are resistant to novobiocin. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Coag negative + novobiocin resistant + UTI = saprophyticus.
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus and a common cause of UTI in young sexually active women.

optionExplanations.A: S epidermidis is coagulase negative but classically novobiocin sensitive.
optionExplanations.B: S aureus is coagulase positive.
optionExplanations.C: Enterococcus is catalase negative.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a coagulase-negative, novobiocin-resistant staphylococcus and a common cause of UTI in young sexually active women.
optionExplanations.E: Group B Streptococcus is catalase negative and CAMP positive.

questions.takeaway: S saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant.
questions.recognition: Use novobiocin to separate saprophyticus from epidermidis.

questions.stem: A tumor becomes hypoxic as it enlarges. Tumor cells increase VEGF transcription and stimulate new-vessel formation. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which molecular change most directly drives this response?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1alpha, which enters the nucleus and promotes expression of adaptive genes including VEGF. VEGF drives the angiogenic switch.

optionExplanations.A: This is a cell-cycle checkpoint effect rather than the hypoxia response.
optionExplanations.B: This would reduce replicative capacity, not stimulate angiogenesis.
optionExplanations.C: This would reduce angiogenesis.
optionExplanations.D: Hypoxia prevents normal HIF-1alpha degradation.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Hypoxia stabilizes HIF-1alpha, which enters the nucleus and promotes expression of adaptive genes including VEGF. VEGF drives the angiogenic switch.

questions.takeaway: Hypoxia → HIF-1alpha stabilization → VEGF.
questions.recognition: Growing tumor + hypoxia + vessels = HIF/VEGF.

questions.stem: The maternal endometrium directly beneath an implanted embryo becomes the maternal component of the mature placenta. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which structure is being described?
questions.hint: Basalis is the “base” under the embryo.
questions.explanation: The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.

optionExplanations.A: This is the remaining decidualized endometrium away from implantation.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The decidua basalis is the maternal endometrium deep to the implanted conceptus and forms the maternal placental component.
optionExplanations.C: The amnion encloses the amniotic cavity and fetus.
optionExplanations.D: This forms the fetal component of the placenta.
optionExplanations.E: This covers the conceptus on the side facing the uterine cavity.

questions.takeaway: Maternal placenta = decidua basalis; fetal placenta = chorion frondosum.
questions.recognition: Questions asking for the maternal placental component point to decidua basalis.

questions.stem: An immunocompromised patient develops pulmonary nodules and brain abscesses. Culture shows thin branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.

optionExplanations.A: Corynebacteria are club-shaped rods, not branching weakly acid-fast filaments.
optionExplanations.B: M tuberculosis is acid-fast but does not form the characteristic branching filamentous morphology.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Nocardia are aerobic branching gram-positive organisms that are weakly acid-fast and cause opportunistic pulmonary disease with potential CNS dissemination.
optionExplanations.D: Streptomyces is filamentous but does not fit the classic opportunistic weakly acid-fast pulmonary/CNS syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Actinomyces is branching gram positive but generally anaerobic and not acid-fast.

questions.takeaway: Nocardia is an aerobic, weakly acid-fast branching bacterium.
questions.recognition: Pulmonary infection with brain abscesses is a classic Nocardia pattern.

questions.stem: An oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus from a respiratory specimen does not ferment glucose, maltose, lactose, or sucrose. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Diplococcus + oxidase positive + no sugars = Moraxella.
questions.explanation: Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.

optionExplanations.A: Pseudomonas is an oxidase-positive gram-negative rod, not a diplococcus.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Moraxella catarrhalis is an oxidase-positive gram-negative diplococcus that is asaccharolytic and is associated with respiratory infections.
optionExplanations.C: N lactamica can ferment glucose, maltose, and lactose.
optionExplanations.D: N meningitidis ferments glucose and maltose.
optionExplanations.E: N gonorrhoeae ferments glucose.

questions.takeaway: Moraxella is asaccharolytic.
questions.recognition: Carbohydrate utilization is a useful way to distinguish Moraxella from Neisseria.

questions.stem: Homologous chromosomes separate normally during gametogenesis, but both sister chromatids of chromosome 18 migrate into the same gamete during the second division. At which stage did nondisjunction occur?
questions.explanation: Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.

optionExplanations.A: Anaphase I separates homologs.
optionExplanations.B: Homolog pairing and recombination occur in prophase I; separation does not.
optionExplanations.C: The segregation error occurs before fertilization.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids. Failure of sister chromatids to separate occurs during anaphase II.
optionExplanations.E: Chromosomes align but do not separate here.

questions.takeaway: Meiosis II nondisjunction is failure of sister chromatids to separate.
questions.recognition: If homologs separated normally but sisters did not, the error is in meiosis II.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin-induced agglutination. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which platelet receptor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.

optionExplanations.A: GpIIb/IIIa deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia with preserved ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.B: PAR-1 is a thrombin receptor and is not the classic defect here.
optionExplanations.C: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A rather than giant platelets and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Bernard-Soulier syndrome results from GpIb deficiency. GpIb binds vWF for platelet adhesion; deficiency causes mucosal bleeding, thrombocytopenia, giant platelets, and abnormal ristocetin response.
optionExplanations.E: P2Y12 is an ADP receptor and antiplatelet-drug target.

questions.takeaway: Bernard-Soulier = GpIb adhesion defect.
questions.recognition: Ristocetin tests vWF-GpIb interaction.

questions.stem: Drug X has a dissociation constant (KD) of 2 nM at a receptor, whereas Drug Y has a KD of 200 nM. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Drug Y must have greater efficacy
Drug X has greater receptor affinity
Drug X must be a full agonist
questions.explanation: KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.

optionExplanations.A: Higher KD means weaker affinity.
optionExplanations.B: KD reflects affinity, not maximal effect.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. KD is inversely related to receptor affinity: a lower KD means less ligand is required to occupy the receptor. Therefore Drug X has greater affinity.
optionExplanations.D: Binding affinity does not establish intrinsic efficacy.
optionExplanations.E: Their KD values differ by 100-fold.

questions.takeaway: KD measures affinity, not efficacy.
questions.recognition: Do not confuse affinity with maximal response.

questions.stem: A young adult has hundreds of adenomatous colonic polyps. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Loss of which tumor-suppressor gene is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: MSH2 is a mismatch-repair gene associated with Lynch syndrome, which usually does not produce hundreds of polyps.
optionExplanations.B: BRCA1 is associated mainly with hereditary breast and ovarian cancer.
optionExplanations.C: Activating RET mutations cause MEN2.
optionExplanations.D: Germline TP53 mutations cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germline loss of APC. APC normally helps regulate beta-catenin; loss promotes excessive Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and epithelial proliferation.

questions.takeaway: FAP = APC loss.
questions.recognition: Polyposis in youth should immediately suggest APC.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer has pain, anxiety, transportation problems, financial stress, and spiritual distress. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which approach best represents holistic patient care?
options: Integrate physical, psychological, social, cultural, and spiritual needs into the care plan
Postpone nonmedical issues until cancer treatment is complete
Refer every concern away without coordinating care
Allow family members to make all decisions
questions.hint: The answer should address the whole person, not one problem.
questions.explanation: Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Holistic care treats the patient as a whole person and integrates physical symptoms with psychological, social, cultural, practical, and spiritual context.
optionExplanations.B: These issues can directly affect current health and treatment adherence.
optionExplanations.C: This addresses only one physical dimension.
optionExplanations.D: Interdisciplinary referrals are valuable, but care must remain integrated.
optionExplanations.E: Patient-centered care prioritizes the capable patient’s own values and preferences.

questions.takeaway: Holistic care integrates multiple dimensions of health.
questions.recognition: If several nonbiologic factors are affecting care, the best answer is integrated care.

questions.stem: A patient develops hemolytic anemia after a medication becomes attached to erythrocyte membranes and IgG binds the drug-associated cell surface. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Type II hypersensitivity occurs when IgG or IgM targets a fixed antigen on a cell surface or tissue, leading to complement activation, opsonization, cell destruction, or altered receptor function.
optionExplanations.B: Type I is IgE-mediated immediate allergy.
optionExplanations.C: Tolerance prevents immune responses rather than producing antibody-mediated cell injury.
optionExplanations.D: Type III involves soluble circulating immune complexes depositing in tissues.
optionExplanations.E: Type IV is T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity.

questions.takeaway: Type II antibodies bind cell-surface or matrix antigens.
questions.recognition: Hemolysis from antibodies coating RBCs is Type II.

questions.stem: A malnourished person drinks a large amount of ethanol without eating and later becomes hypoglycemic. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which biochemical change most directly inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis?
options: Increased NADH drives pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate
questions.hint: Think redox state: ethanol raises NADH.
questions.explanation: Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Ethanol metabolism increases, rather than decreases, NADH.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the reason gluconeogenesis fails after ethanol ingestion.
optionExplanations.C: Glucagon instead favors gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.D: The central mechanism is the altered NADH/NAD+ redox ratio.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Ethanol oxidation generates excess NADH. High NADH shifts pyruvate toward lactate and oxaloacetate toward malate, depleting substrates needed for gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Excess NADH diverts pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis.
questions.recognition: Fasting + alcohol + hypoglycemia is a redox problem.

questions.stem: A teenager develops exercise-induced muscle cramps and myoglobinuria. After a brief rest, exercise becomes easier. Lactate fails to rise normally during a forearm exercise test. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: McArdle disease is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Skeletal muscle cannot efficiently mobilize glycogen during intense exercise, causing cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and the second-wind phenomenon.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. McArdle disease is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency. Skeletal muscle cannot efficiently mobilize glycogen during intense exercise, causing cramps, rhabdomyolysis, and the second-wind phenomenon.
optionExplanations.B: This causes a hepatic glycogen-storage disorder rather than exercise-induced muscle symptoms.
optionExplanations.C: Andersen disease causes abnormal glycogen and progressive liver disease.
optionExplanations.D: Cori disease primarily causes hepatic manifestations.
optionExplanations.E: This causes severe fasting hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly.

questions.takeaway: McArdle = muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency.
questions.recognition: If lactate does not rise with exercise, think a block in muscle glycogen use.

questions.stem: A patient with acute pancreatitis develops chalky white deposits within peripancreatic adipose tissue. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which type of necrosis produced this finding?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic lipases digest surrounding adipose triglycerides. Released fatty acids bind calcium and produce chalky saponification deposits, the classic appearance of enzymatic fat necrosis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Pancreatic lipases digest surrounding adipose triglycerides. Released fatty acids bind calcium and produce chalky saponification deposits, the classic appearance of enzymatic fat necrosis.
optionExplanations.B: This is typical of ischemic injury in most solid organs.
optionExplanations.C: This is classically associated with tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.D: This occurs in brain infarcts and many abscesses.
optionExplanations.E: This is a vascular-wall necrosis pattern.

questions.takeaway: Fat necrosis in pancreatitis reflects lipase-mediated saponification.
questions.recognition: If the stem says chalky white peripancreatic deposits, the answer is fat necrosis.

questions.stem: A child has chronic jaundice, splenomegaly, pigment gallstones, and spherocytes. The direct antiglobulin test is negative, and a parent had the same condition. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which defect is most likely?
questions.hint: Inherited spherocytes + negative DAT = hereditary spherocytosis.
questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects in RBC membrane-skeleton proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Membrane loss produces poorly deformable spherocytes cleared in the spleen.

optionExplanations.A: Warm autoimmune hemolysis is usually DAT positive and not inherited in this pattern.
optionExplanations.B: This is sickle-cell disease and produces sickled cells rather than hereditary spherocytes.
optionExplanations.C: This is a coagulation disorder, not a hemolytic anemia.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hereditary spherocytosis is caused by defects in RBC membrane-skeleton proteins such as spectrin, ankyrin, or band 3. Membrane loss produces poorly deformable spherocytes cleared in the spleen.
optionExplanations.E: This produces oxidant-triggered bite cells/Heinz bodies.

questions.takeaway: Hereditary spherocytosis is a membrane-cytoskeleton disorder.
questions.recognition: Always use DAT to separate hereditary from immune spherocytosis.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain says, “The pain is still present, but I know I can work, exercise, and care for my family even when it hurts.”. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which psychological construct is demonstrated?
questions.hint: Confidence in functioning despite pain = self-efficacy.
questions.explanation: Pain self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function and continue valued activities despite pain.

optionExplanations.A: Hypervigilance is excessive monitoring of pain sensations.
optionExplanations.B: Fear avoidance involves restricting activity because movement is believed to cause harm.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pain self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function and continue valued activities despite pain.
optionExplanations.D: Catastrophizing involves rumination, magnification, and helplessness.
optionExplanations.E: Helplessness is a maladaptive belief that one cannot cope.

questions.takeaway: Pain self-efficacy is adaptive confidence, not absence of pain.
questions.recognition: The patient is describing function despite symptoms.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman receives a drug that blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase. Intracellular sodium rises and the transmembrane sodium gradient falls. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which normal transport stoichiometry is directly inhibited?
options: 1 Na+ out and 1 K+ in per ATP
3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in per ATP
2 Na+ out and 3 K+ in per ATP
3 Na+ in and 2 K+ out per ATP
2 Na+ out and 2 K+ in without ATP
questions.hint: Remember the classic “3 out, 2 in, 1 ATP” rule.
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+-ATPase hydrolyzes one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+. The unequal charge movement makes the pump electrogenic and establishes the sodium gradient used by many secondary transporters.

optionExplanations.A: The pump moves three sodium ions out and two potassium ions in.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The Na+/K+-ATPase hydrolyzes one ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+. The unequal charge movement makes the pump electrogenic and establishes the sodium gradient used by many secondary transporters.
optionExplanations.C: This reverses the normal stoichiometry.
optionExplanations.D: This reverses the direction of both ions.
optionExplanations.E: The pump is primary active transport and requires ATP.

questions.takeaway: Na+/K+-ATPase = 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in, 1 ATP.
questions.recognition: Ouabain/digoxin + rising intracellular Na+ should trigger the Na+/K+ pump stoichiometry.

questions.stem: A researcher analyzes normal decidual leukocytes in early pregnancy. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which population is most abundant?
questions.hint: The dominant decidual immune cell is an innate lymphocyte.
questions.explanation: Specialized uterine natural killer cells are the dominant leukocyte population in healthy early decidua and participate in trophoblast interaction and vascular remodeling.

optionExplanations.A: Plasma cells are not predominant.
optionExplanations.B: B cells are not the dominant decidual leukocyte population.
optionExplanations.C: Eosinophils are not the major normal decidual population.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Specialized uterine natural killer cells are the dominant leukocyte population in healthy early decidua and participate in trophoblast interaction and vascular remodeling.
optionExplanations.E: Neutrophils are important in acute inflammation but are not the dominant normal decidual leukocyte population.

questions.takeaway: Uterine NK cells dominate the decidua.
questions.recognition: Pregnancy-immunology cell-frequency questions usually point to NK cells.

questions.stem: A clinical trial concludes that a drug is superior to placebo even though there is actually no true treatment effect and the null hypothesis is correct. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which statistical error occurred?
questions.explanation: A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis—concluding that a difference exists when it does not. Its probability is alpha.

optionExplanations.A: Lead-time bias is a screening-survival artifact.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis—concluding that a difference exists when it does not. Its probability is alpha.
optionExplanations.C: Confounding is distortion by a third variable, not this hypothesis-testing error.
optionExplanations.D: Recall bias involves differential memory of past exposures.
optionExplanations.E: Type II error is failure to detect a real effect.

questions.takeaway: Type I error: reject a true null; probability = alpha.
questions.recognition: If the study “finds” an effect that is not real, think Type I error.

questions.stem: A patient with tuberculosis receives rifampin. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which bacterial enzyme is directly inhibited?
questions.explanation: Rifampin binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and inhibits transcription. It is also a strong hepatic enzyme inducer.

optionExplanations.A: Several protein-synthesis inhibitors target the 50S subunit.
optionExplanations.B: Beta-lactamase inhibitors target this resistance enzyme, not rifampin.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Rifampin binds bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and inhibits transcription. It is also a strong hepatic enzyme inducer.
optionExplanations.D: Sulfonamides inhibit this enzyme.
optionExplanations.E: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase.

questions.takeaway: Rifampin inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
questions.recognition: TB drug + orange fluids/enzyme induction often points to rifampin.

questions.stem: A patient develops diffuse rash, watery diarrhea, and hepatitis several weeks after allogeneic hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which immune process is responsible?
options: Immune complexes deposit in the graft
Recipient antibodies attack donor stem cells
Donor T cells attack recipient tissues
questions.hint: Remember the direction: graft attacks host.
questions.explanation: Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient tissues as foreign. Skin, GI tract, and liver are classic targets.

optionExplanations.A: This is Type I hypersensitivity, not GVHD.
optionExplanations.B: Neutrophils are not the principal effector cells of GVHD.
optionExplanations.C: This is not the primary mechanism of GVHD.
optionExplanations.D: That describes host-versus-graft rejection rather than graft-versus-host disease.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Graft-versus-host disease occurs when immunocompetent donor T lymphocytes recognize recipient tissues as foreign. Skin, GI tract, and liver are classic targets.

questions.takeaway: GVHD = donor T cells attacking recipient tissues.
questions.recognition: Stem-cell transplant + rash + diarrhea + hepatitis = GVHD.

questions.stem: A cervical biopsy shows severe atypia throughout the full epithelial thickness, but the basement membrane is intact. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which diagnosis best describes this lesion?
questions.hint: Full thickness + intact basement membrane = in situ.
questions.explanation: Carcinoma in situ is full-thickness epithelial dysplasia without invasion through the basement membrane. Breach of the basement membrane defines invasive carcinoma.

optionExplanations.A: Metaplasia is replacement of one mature cell type by another without full-thickness malignant atypia.
optionExplanations.B: Hypertrophy is increased cell size rather than dysplastic epithelial growth.
optionExplanations.C: Invasive carcinoma requires breach of the basement membrane.
optionExplanations.D: Hyperplasia increases cell number while preserving orderly architecture.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Carcinoma in situ is full-thickness epithelial dysplasia without invasion through the basement membrane. Breach of the basement membrane defines invasive carcinoma.

questions.takeaway: Carcinoma in situ has not invaded the basement membrane.
questions.recognition: The basement membrane is the dividing line between in situ and invasive carcinoma.

questions.stem: A malignant cell line takes up large amounts of glucose and converts pyruvate to lactate despite adequate oxygen and intact mitochondria. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which phenomenon is present?
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.

optionExplanations.A: The Cori cycle transfers lactate to liver for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.B: Beta-oxidation degrades fatty acids in mitochondria.
optionExplanations.C: The respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species in phagocytes.
optionExplanations.D: Ketogenesis produces ketone bodies during fasting states.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.

questions.takeaway: Warburg effect = aerobic glycolysis.
questions.recognition: FDG-PET works partly because many tumors avidly consume glucose.

questions.stem: A patient with invasive fungal disease receives an azole. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which fungal enzyme is inhibited?
questions.hint: Azoles block ergosterol synthesis, not the cell wall.
questions.explanation: Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.

optionExplanations.A: This is the echinocandin target.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.
optionExplanations.C: This is inhibited by terbinafine.
optionExplanations.D: Polyenes bind ergosterol rather than inhibiting its synthesis enzyme.
optionExplanations.E: This is a bacterial cell-wall target.

questions.takeaway: Azoles inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase.
questions.recognition: Membrane sterol synthesis + CYP inhibition = azole.

questions.stem: A patient develops bite cells and Heinz bodies after taking an oxidizing medication. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which biochemical defect most directly causes the erythrocyte injury?
options: Decreased NADPH production with impaired regeneration of reduced glutathione
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.

optionExplanations.A: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and do not use the TCA cycle.
optionExplanations.B: This causes vitamin B12 deficiency.
optionExplanations.C: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.
optionExplanations.D: This is the mechanism of thalassemia.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency impairs antioxidant defense in RBCs.
questions.recognition: Oxidant drug + bite cells/Heinz bodies = G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient repeatedly misses chemotherapy because of job loss, gasoline costs, and risk of eviction. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which interdisciplinary team member is best suited to address these barriers?
questions.hint: Match the referral to the barrier.
questions.explanation: Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.
optionExplanations.B: A speech therapist addresses communication and swallowing rehabilitation.
optionExplanations.C: A radiation physicist supports technical radiation planning and safety.
optionExplanations.D: A pathologist focuses on tissue and laboratory diagnosis.
optionExplanations.E: A dermatologist treats skin disease rather than primary housing/transportation barriers.

questions.takeaway: Social work addresses housing, transportation, finances, and resource access.
questions.recognition: If the problem is access rather than biology, think social work.

questions.stem: Repeated measurements of the same reference sample are nearly identical, but all are consistently 15% above the true value. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. How should this assay be described?
questions.hint: Precise but wrong = reliable, not valid.
questions.explanation: Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.

optionExplanations.A: The assay is precise but not accurate.
optionExplanations.B: Reliability is high because measurements are tightly reproducible.
optionExplanations.C: Sensitivity and specificity describe diagnostic classification, not measurement accuracy/precision.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.
optionExplanations.E: The measurements are consistent but inaccurate, the opposite pattern.

questions.takeaway: Reliability = precision; validity = accuracy.
questions.recognition: Tight cluster away from truth is high reliability, low validity.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is heterozygous for an autosomal dominant pathogenic allele with 80% penetrance. The partner does not carry the allele. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What is the probability that their next child will develop the disease?
questions.explanation: The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.

optionExplanations.A: This is penetrance among those who inherit the allele, not the overall child risk.
optionExplanations.B: This is the transmission probability before accounting for penetrance.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.
optionExplanations.D: This is the classic affected-child risk for two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder.
optionExplanations.E: This does not correctly combine 50% transmission with 80% penetrance.

questions.takeaway: Reduced penetrance lowers observed disease risk below genotype transmission risk.
questions.recognition: For autosomal dominant disease with incomplete penetrance, do not stop at 50%.

questions.stem: A patient has acute leukemia with abnormal promyelocytes, numerous Auer rods, and DIC. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which treatment should be initiated urgently?
questions.hint: Promyelocytes + Auer rods + DIC = APL = ATRA.
questions.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.
optionExplanations.B: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL and is classically used in CML.
optionExplanations.C: Hydroxyurea can lower high leukocyte counts but does not correct the PML-RARA differentiation block.
optionExplanations.D: Erythropoietin does not treat acute leukemia or DIC.
optionExplanations.E: Rituximab targets CD20-positive B-cell malignancies.

questions.takeaway: ATRA is urgent differentiation therapy for APL.
questions.recognition: APL is one of the leukemia diagnoses where immediate targeted therapy matters.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman takes an oral medication that has a volume of distribution of 50 L, a desired plasma concentration of 8 mg/L, and oral bioavailability of 50%. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What loading dose is required?
questions.hint: Calculate the systemic requirement first, then divide by F.
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.

optionExplanations.A: This overcorrects for incomplete bioavailability.
optionExplanations.B: This would be the dose if bioavailability were 100%.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.
optionExplanations.D: This underestimates the dose and effectively multiplies rather than divides by bioavailability.
optionExplanations.E: This does not follow the loading-dose relationship.

questions.takeaway: Loading dose depends on Vd, target concentration, and bioavailability.
questions.recognition: If oral F is below 1, the administered loading dose must be larger than the systemic requirement.

questions.stem: A teenager has recurrent meningococcal infections with otherwise normal immune function. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which immune defect is most likely?
options: Deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5-C9)
questions.explanation: Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.

optionExplanations.A: C3 deficiency causes broader susceptibility to pyogenic encapsulated infections.
optionExplanations.B: This is a bleeding disorder, not an immune defect.
optionExplanations.C: MPO deficiency does not produce the classic recurrent meningococcal pattern.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
optionExplanations.E: IgE deficiency does not classically cause recurrent Neisseria.

questions.takeaway: C5-C9 deficiency → recurrent Neisseria.
questions.recognition: Repeated meningococcal infection is the classic board clue for MAC deficiency.

questions.stem: A blastocyst has formed after cleavage and morula stages. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. When does implantation normally begin?
questions.explanation: Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.

optionExplanations.A: Implantation begins much earlier.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.
optionExplanations.C: Placental and fetal circulation develop after implantation begins.
optionExplanations.D: This is far too late.
optionExplanations.E: The conceptus must first undergo cleavage and blastocyst formation.

questions.takeaway: Implantation begins around the end of the first week.
questions.recognition: Blastocyst stage means implantation is imminent.

questions.stem: A palpable breast mass is firm and irregular. Ultrasound is suspicious, but mammography is negative. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No further evaluation because mammography is negative
questions.hint: Suspicious mass beats a negative screening test.
questions.explanation: A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.

optionExplanations.A: This would inappropriately delay diagnosis.
optionExplanations.B: FNA gives cytology but less tissue architecture; core biopsy is preferred for a suspicious solid lesion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.
optionExplanations.D: A negative mammogram does not override a suspicious mass and ultrasound.
optionExplanations.E: Suspicious clinical and ultrasound findings require tissue diagnosis.

questions.takeaway: Suspicious solid breast lesion → core needle biopsy.
questions.recognition: Never let a negative mammogram cancel a concerning palpable/ultrasound finding.

questions.stem: A newborn with meningitis has beta-hemolytic catalase-negative gram-positive cocci. Hemolysis is enhanced adjacent to Staphylococcus aureus on agar. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

optionExplanations.A: S pneumoniae is alpha hemolytic and optochin sensitive.
optionExplanations.B: Staphylococci are catalase positive.
optionExplanations.C: Group A Streptococcus is beta hemolytic but is not CAMP positive.
optionExplanations.D: Enterococcus is typically bile-esculin positive and grows in 6.5% NaCl.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

questions.takeaway: S agalactiae is CAMP positive.
questions.recognition: Neonatal meningitis plus enhanced hemolysis is a classic GBS clue.

questions.stem: A patient develops urticaria, wheezing, facial swelling, and hypotension within minutes of peanut exposure. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which immune mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

optionExplanations.A: This is a Type II mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: This is a Type III mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: This is Type IV hypersensitivity and develops over a longer interval.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.
optionExplanations.E: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection rather than causing this immediate allergic syndrome.

questions.takeaway: Type I = IgE + mast cells.
questions.recognition: Rapid hypotension and wheezing after exposure is anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A newborn has distal intestinal aganglionosis and fails to pass meconium. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which developmental process failed?
options: Migration of neural crest cells into the hindgut
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.

optionExplanations.A: Intermediate mesoderm forms urogenital structures, not enteric neurons.
optionExplanations.B: The notochord organizes axial development but does not directly populate enteric ganglia.
optionExplanations.C: Persistence can produce sacrococcygeal teratoma.
optionExplanations.D: Failure causes neural-tube defects, not enteric aganglionosis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.

questions.takeaway: Hirschsprung = failed neural crest migration.
questions.recognition: Newborn obstruction + absent ganglion cells is a neural-crest question.

questions.stem: A sarcoma amplifies MDM2. TP53 is structurally normal, but p53 protein concentrations are markedly reduced. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which molecular event explains this finding?
options: Increased ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of p53
questions.explanation: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.

optionExplanations.A: MDM2 lowers p53 protein rather than increasing it.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.
optionExplanations.C: BAX is a proapoptotic p53 target and would not explain low p53.
optionExplanations.D: Reduced p53 lowers p21 induction.
optionExplanations.E: MDM2 does not primarily suppress BCL2.

questions.takeaway: MDM2 ubiquitinates p53.
questions.recognition: Wild-type TP53 with low p53 protein suggests excessive MDM2 activity.

questions.stem: A patient with untreated HIV has a CD4 count of 150/µL, progressive dyspnea, nonproductive cough, fever, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.

optionExplanations.A: CMV classically causes retinitis, esophagitis, or colitis at very low CD4 counts.
optionExplanations.B: Cryptococcus is a classic cause of meningitis in advanced HIV.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
optionExplanations.D: Toxoplasma most classically causes CNS lesions and neurologic findings.
optionExplanations.E: MAC typically appears at more profound immunosuppression and often causes disseminated disease.

questions.takeaway: Pneumocystis is the classic pulmonary OI below 200 CD4 cells/µL.
questions.recognition: Use CD4 thresholds as pattern-recognition anchors.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent hemarthroses. PT is normal, aPTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing, and factor VIII activity is markedly reduced. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: Deep bleeding + VIII deficiency = Hemophilia A.
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.

optionExplanations.A: This is a platelet-adhesion defect with giant platelets.
optionExplanations.B: Hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.
optionExplanations.C: Factor XII deficiency can prolong aPTT but usually does not cause clinical bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.
optionExplanations.E: vWD more often causes mucocutaneous bleeding and abnormal platelet adhesion.

questions.takeaway: Hemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency.
questions.recognition: Hemarthroses are a secondary-hemostasis clue.

questions.stem: Genetic analysis of a trisomic conceptus shows that both homologous maternal chromosomes were transmitted into the same oocyte. Which meiotic error occurred?
options: Failure of DNA replication in S phase
questions.explanation: Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.
optionExplanations.B: Recombination abnormalities can predispose to nondisjunction but do not themselves describe both homologs entering one gamete.
optionExplanations.C: Meiosis II errors involve sister chromatids rather than homologous chromosomes.
optionExplanations.D: Postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction generally produces mosaicism.
optionExplanations.E: Replication failure is not chromosome nondisjunction.

questions.takeaway: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes.
questions.recognition: If the stem explicitly says “both homologs,” choose meiosis I.

questions.stem: A receptor has constitutive activity even in the absence of ligand. A new drug binds the receptor and reduces signaling below the basal level. Which term best describes this drug?
questions.hint: The key phrase is “below basal activity.”
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.

optionExplanations.A: A partial agonist still increases activity above baseline, though less than a full agonist.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.
optionExplanations.C: A full agonist increases receptor signaling.
optionExplanations.D: A positive allosteric modulator enhances receptor responsiveness.
optionExplanations.E: A neutral antagonist blocks agonists but does not reduce constitutive activity.

questions.takeaway: Inverse agonist = negative efficacy at a constitutively active receptor.
questions.recognition: Constitutive activity plus a drug that lowers the baseline points to an inverse agonist.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman is exercising intensely. Cellular ATP falls while AMP rises. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme is most directly activated to increase glycolytic flux?
questions.explanation: AMP signals a low-energy state and activates PFK-1, the key committed regulatory enzyme of glycolysis, thereby increasing ATP production.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. AMP signals a low-energy state and activates PFK-1, the key committed regulatory enzyme of glycolysis, thereby increasing ATP production.
optionExplanations.B: This enzyme catalyzes a gluconeogenic/anaplerotic reaction.
optionExplanations.C: This is a gluconeogenic enzyme.
optionExplanations.D: AMP inhibits this gluconeogenic enzyme.
optionExplanations.E: This enzyme supports hepatic glucose release rather than glycolysis.

questions.takeaway: AMP activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
questions.recognition: PFK-1 is the high-yield glycolytic checkpoint for low-energy states.
