questions.stem: A patient has anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, and reticulocytosis after mechanical heart-valve placement. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which additional finding most strongly supports intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.

optionExplanations.A: Splenomegaly is more strongly associated with chronic extravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.
optionExplanations.C: Ferritin is nonspecific and does not directly identify intravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.D: Erythropoietin generally rises in response to anemia.
optionExplanations.E: This can occur in hereditary spherocytosis but is not the best marker of intravascular destruction.

questions.takeaway: Intravascular hemolysis lowers haptoglobin.
questions.recognition: Mechanical hemolysis plus low haptoglobin fits intravascular destruction.

questions.stem: A patient develops jaundice and dark urine after an oxidant drug. Smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.

optionExplanations.A: This causes microcytic anemia without oxidant-triggered hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: This causes spherocytes due to membrane-skeleton defects.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.
optionExplanations.D: This causes microcytosis from reduced beta-globin synthesis.
optionExplanations.E: This causes DAT-positive spherocytic hemolysis.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis.
questions.recognition: Bite cells are a classic post-Heinz-body clue.

questions.stem: A growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase. GRB2 and SOS activate Ras. Which downstream sequence most directly promotes proliferative gene transcription?
questions.hint: Think of the classic MAPK kinase cascade.
questions.explanation: The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: Smad signaling is associated with TGF-beta receptors and does not proceed through Gq.
optionExplanations.B: JAK/STAT is a cytokine-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.C: PI3K signals mainly through PIP3 and AKT, not caspase-8.
optionExplanations.D: This is a GPCR pathway.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.

questions.takeaway: RTK/GRB2/SOS → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK.
questions.recognition: A Ras question usually wants the MAPK cascade.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced illness asks how hospice differs from palliative care. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Hospice and palliative care are identical
Palliative care cannot be given during chemotherapy
Hospice generally serves patients with an estimated prognosis of about 6 months or less
Hospice requires expected death within 24 hours
questions.hint: Hospice is the narrower end-of-life model.
questions.explanation: Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.

optionExplanations.A: Hospice addresses many physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs.
optionExplanations.B: Palliative care is broader and can occur much earlier.
optionExplanations.C: Palliative care can be concurrent with disease-directed treatment.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.
optionExplanations.E: Hospice is not limited to the final day of life.

questions.takeaway: Hospice is generally associated with a prognosis of about 6 months or less.
questions.recognition: Palliative care is broad; hospice has a more specific end-of-life eligibility framework.

questions.stem: A patient develops an intensely pruritic rash 48 hours after nickel exposure. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.

optionExplanations.A: Type I reactions are immediate rather than delayed by 48 hours.
optionExplanations.B: Complement deficiency does not produce contact dermatitis.
optionExplanations.C: Type II targets fixed antigens with IgG/IgM.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.
optionExplanations.E: Type III involves soluble immune complexes.

questions.takeaway: Type IV = delayed, T-cell mediated.
questions.recognition: Nickel and poison ivy are classic Type IV triggers.

questions.stem: An infant has severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and marked hepatomegaly. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly = GSD I.
questions.explanation: Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.B: Deficiency causes McArdle disease with exercise intolerance.
optionExplanations.C: Deficiency causes Andersen disease with abnormal glycogen and cirrhosis.
optionExplanations.D: Deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia.
optionExplanations.E: Deficiency causes Cori disease, which is generally milder and preserves gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Von Gierke = glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.
questions.recognition: If both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis fail at the final step, think G6Pase.

questions.stem: A renal artery thrombosis causes an infarct. Days later, dead renal tubules retain their general architectural outlines despite loss of nuclei. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which pattern of necrosis is present?
questions.hint: Most solid-organ infarcts coagulate; brain liquefies.
questions.explanation: Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.

optionExplanations.A: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain infarction and many abscesses.
optionExplanations.B: Fat necrosis occurs in settings such as acute pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.
optionExplanations.D: Caseous necrosis is classically associated with tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.E: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in damaged vessel walls, such as vasculitis.

questions.takeaway: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture for a time.
questions.recognition: Kidney/heart/spleen infarct = coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender firm uterus. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.
optionExplanations.B: Previa typically causes painless bleeding.
optionExplanations.C: Cervical insufficiency usually causes painless dilation in the second trimester.
optionExplanations.D: A partial mole is a triploid abnormal gestation and does not fit this late-pregnancy emergency.
optionExplanations.E: Accreta presents mainly as abnormal placental adherence and postpartum hemorrhage.

questions.takeaway: Abruption causes painful bleeding and a tender/firm uterus.
questions.recognition: Pain + bleeding + firm uterus is a classic triad.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man develops right-sided colon cancer. Several first-degree relatives developed colon or endometrial cancer before age 50, and tumor testing shows microsatellite instability. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which DNA repair system is defective?
questions.hint: Family history + right colon/endometrium + MSI = mismatch repair.
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

optionExplanations.A: BER repairs small altered bases rather than replication mismatches.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the pathway responsible for Lynch syndrome.
optionExplanations.C: NER is associated with bulky DNA lesions and xeroderma pigmentosum.
optionExplanations.D: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome = defective DNA mismatch repair.
questions.recognition: Microsatellite instability is the biochemical fingerprint of mismatch-repair failure.

questions.stem: A patient with MRSA bacteremia receives vancomycin. There is no history suggesting an alternative acquired cause. Which bacterial structure does the drug bind?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.

optionExplanations.A: This is targeted by aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.
optionExplanations.C: This is inhibited by rifampin.
optionExplanations.D: This is targeted by fluoroquinolones.
optionExplanations.E: This is inhibited by trimethoprim.

questions.takeaway: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala.
questions.recognition: Differentiate vancomycin from beta-lactams: substrate binding versus PBP binding.

questions.stem: A patient develops bite cells and Heinz bodies after taking an oxidizing medication. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which biochemical defect most directly causes the erythrocyte injury?
options: Decreased NADPH production with impaired regeneration of reduced glutathione
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces pentose-phosphate-pathway NADPH production. Without adequate NADPH, erythrocytes cannot maintain glutathione in its reduced antioxidant form and become vulnerable to oxidative damage.
optionExplanations.B: This is the mechanism of thalassemia.
optionExplanations.C: This causes vitamin B12 deficiency.
optionExplanations.D: Mature erythrocytes lack mitochondria and do not use the TCA cycle.
optionExplanations.E: Spectrin defects cause hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency impairs antioxidant defense in RBCs.
questions.recognition: Oxidant drug + bite cells/Heinz bodies = G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man is heterozygous for an autosomal dominant pathogenic allele with 80% penetrance. The partner does not carry the allele. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What is the probability that their next child will develop the disease?
questions.explanation: The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.

optionExplanations.A: This is penetrance among those who inherit the allele, not the overall child risk.
optionExplanations.B: This does not correctly combine 50% transmission with 80% penetrance.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The child has a 50% chance of inheriting the dominant allele, and an 80% chance of expressing disease if the allele is inherited. 0.5 × 0.8 = 0.4, or 40%.
optionExplanations.D: This is the classic affected-child risk for two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder.
optionExplanations.E: This is the transmission probability before accounting for penetrance.

questions.takeaway: Reduced penetrance lowers observed disease risk below genotype transmission risk.
questions.recognition: For autosomal dominant disease with incomplete penetrance, do not stop at 50%.

questions.stem: A blastocyst has formed after cleavage and morula stages. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. When does implantation normally begin?
questions.explanation: Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.

optionExplanations.A: This is far too late.
optionExplanations.B: The conceptus must first undergo cleavage and blastocyst formation.
optionExplanations.C: Placental and fetal circulation develop after implantation begins.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5 and implantation normally begins around days 5–7 after fertilization.
optionExplanations.E: Implantation begins much earlier.

questions.takeaway: Implantation begins around the end of the first week.
questions.recognition: Blastocyst stage means implantation is imminent.

questions.stem: Repeated measurements of the same reference sample are nearly identical, but all are consistently 15% above the true value. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. How should this assay be described?
questions.hint: Precise but wrong = reliable, not valid.
questions.explanation: Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Reliability refers to precision and reproducibility; validity refers to accuracy relative to the true value. These measurements are highly reproducible but systematically biased.
optionExplanations.B: Sensitivity and specificity describe diagnostic classification, not measurement accuracy/precision.
optionExplanations.C: The assay is precise but not accurate.
optionExplanations.D: Reliability is high because measurements are tightly reproducible.
optionExplanations.E: The measurements are consistent but inaccurate, the opposite pattern.

questions.takeaway: Reliability = precision; validity = accuracy.
questions.recognition: Tight cluster away from truth is high reliability, low validity.

questions.stem: A patient with invasive fungal disease receives an azole. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which fungal enzyme is inhibited?
questions.hint: Azoles block ergosterol synthesis, not the cell wall.
questions.explanation: Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.

optionExplanations.A: This is inhibited by terbinafine.
optionExplanations.B: This is the echinocandin target.
optionExplanations.C: Polyenes bind ergosterol rather than inhibiting its synthesis enzyme.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Azoles inhibit fungal CYP-dependent 14-alpha-demethylase, decreasing ergosterol synthesis and disrupting fungal membrane function.
optionExplanations.E: This is a bacterial cell-wall target.

questions.takeaway: Azoles inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase.
questions.recognition: Membrane sterol synthesis + CYP inhibition = azole.

questions.stem: A malignant cell line takes up large amounts of glucose and converts pyruvate to lactate despite adequate oxygen and intact mitochondria. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which phenomenon is present?
questions.explanation: The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.

optionExplanations.A: The respiratory burst generates reactive oxygen species in phagocytes.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The Warburg effect is aerobic glycolysis: cancer cells preferentially use high rates of glucose uptake and lactate production even when oxygen is available.
optionExplanations.C: Ketogenesis produces ketone bodies during fasting states.
optionExplanations.D: The Cori cycle transfers lactate to liver for gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.E: Beta-oxidation degrades fatty acids in mitochondria.

questions.takeaway: Warburg effect = aerobic glycolysis.
questions.recognition: FDG-PET works partly because many tumors avidly consume glucose.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman takes an oral medication that has a volume of distribution of 50 L, a desired plasma concentration of 8 mg/L, and oral bioavailability of 50%. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What loading dose is required?
questions.hint: Calculate the systemic requirement first, then divide by F.
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.

optionExplanations.A: This does not follow the loading-dose relationship.
optionExplanations.B: This overcorrects for incomplete bioavailability.
optionExplanations.C: This underestimates the dose and effectively multiplies rather than divides by bioavailability.
optionExplanations.D: This would be the dose if bioavailability were 100%.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Loading dose = Vd × target concentration / bioavailability. Here, 50 L × 8 mg/L = 400 mg systemically; dividing by 0.5 gives 800 mg orally.

questions.takeaway: Loading dose depends on Vd, target concentration, and bioavailability.
questions.recognition: If oral F is below 1, the administered loading dose must be larger than the systemic requirement.

questions.stem: A patient has acute leukemia with abnormal promyelocytes, numerous Auer rods, and DIC. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which treatment should be initiated urgently?
questions.hint: Promyelocytes + Auer rods + DIC = APL = ATRA.
questions.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.

optionExplanations.A: Erythropoietin does not treat acute leukemia or DIC.
optionExplanations.B: Hydroxyurea can lower high leukocyte counts but does not correct the PML-RARA differentiation block.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is associated with PML-RARA and a high risk of fatal DIC. ATRA relieves the differentiation block and should be started as soon as APL is strongly suspected.
optionExplanations.D: Imatinib targets BCR-ABL and is classically used in CML.
optionExplanations.E: Rituximab targets CD20-positive B-cell malignancies.

questions.takeaway: ATRA is urgent differentiation therapy for APL.
questions.recognition: APL is one of the leukemia diagnoses where immediate targeted therapy matters.

questions.stem: A teenager has recurrent meningococcal infections with otherwise normal immune function. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which immune defect is most likely?
options: Deficiency of a terminal complement component (C5-C9)
questions.explanation: Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.

optionExplanations.A: MPO deficiency does not produce the classic recurrent meningococcal pattern.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Deficiency of C5-C9 prevents normal membrane-attack-complex formation and strongly predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections.
optionExplanations.C: C3 deficiency causes broader susceptibility to pyogenic encapsulated infections.
optionExplanations.D: IgE deficiency does not classically cause recurrent Neisseria.
optionExplanations.E: This is a bleeding disorder, not an immune defect.

questions.takeaway: C5-C9 deficiency → recurrent Neisseria.
questions.recognition: Repeated meningococcal infection is the classic board clue for MAC deficiency.

questions.stem: A patient repeatedly misses chemotherapy because of job loss, gasoline costs, and risk of eviction. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which interdisciplinary team member is best suited to address these barriers?
questions.hint: Match the referral to the barrier.
questions.explanation: Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.

optionExplanations.A: A speech therapist addresses communication and swallowing rehabilitation.
optionExplanations.B: A radiation physicist supports technical radiation planning and safety.
optionExplanations.C: A dermatologist treats skin disease rather than primary housing/transportation barriers.
optionExplanations.D: A pathologist focuses on tissue and laboratory diagnosis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Social workers help address practical social determinants such as housing, transportation, finances, insurance, and connection to community resources.

questions.takeaway: Social work addresses housing, transportation, finances, and resource access.
questions.recognition: If the problem is access rather than biology, think social work.

options: Failure of DNA replication in S phase
questions.explanation: Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Meiosis I normally separates homologous chromosomes. If both maternal homologs travel to the same daughter cell, the error is meiosis I nondisjunction.
optionExplanations.B: Replication failure is not chromosome nondisjunction.
optionExplanations.C: Meiosis II errors involve sister chromatids rather than homologous chromosomes.
optionExplanations.D: Recombination abnormalities can predispose to nondisjunction but do not themselves describe both homologs entering one gamete.
optionExplanations.E: Postzygotic mitotic nondisjunction generally produces mosaicism.

questions.recognition: If the stem explicitly says “both homologs,” choose meiosis I.

questions.stem: A newborn with meningitis has beta-hemolytic catalase-negative gram-positive cocci. Hemolysis is enhanced adjacent to Staphylococcus aureus on agar. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.

optionExplanations.A: Staphylococci are catalase positive.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) is CAMP positive, producing enhanced hemolysis near S aureus. It is a major cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis.
optionExplanations.C: Group A Streptococcus is beta hemolytic but is not CAMP positive.
optionExplanations.D: S pneumoniae is alpha hemolytic and optochin sensitive.
optionExplanations.E: Enterococcus is typically bile-esculin positive and grows in 6.5% NaCl.

questions.takeaway: S agalactiae is CAMP positive.
questions.recognition: Neonatal meningitis plus enhanced hemolysis is a classic GBS clue.

questions.stem: A palpable breast mass is firm and irregular. Ultrasound is suspicious, but mammography is negative. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: No further evaluation because mammography is negative
questions.hint: Suspicious mass beats a negative screening test.
questions.explanation: A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. A persistent suspicious solid breast lesion requires tissue diagnosis even when mammography is negative. Core needle biopsy provides histology and tissue architecture.
optionExplanations.B: Suspicious clinical and ultrasound findings require tissue diagnosis.
optionExplanations.C: FNA gives cytology but less tissue architecture; core biopsy is preferred for a suspicious solid lesion.
optionExplanations.D: This would inappropriately delay diagnosis.
optionExplanations.E: A negative mammogram does not override a suspicious mass and ultrasound.

questions.takeaway: Suspicious solid breast lesion → core needle biopsy.
questions.recognition: Never let a negative mammogram cancel a concerning palpable/ultrasound finding.

questions.stem: A sarcoma amplifies MDM2. TP53 is structurally normal, but p53 protein concentrations are markedly reduced. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which molecular event explains this finding?
options: Increased ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of p53
questions.explanation: MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.

optionExplanations.A: BAX is a proapoptotic p53 target and would not explain low p53.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. MDM2 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets p53 for proteasomal degradation. Amplification can therefore create functional p53 deficiency without TP53 mutation.
optionExplanations.C: Reduced p53 lowers p21 induction.
optionExplanations.D: MDM2 lowers p53 protein rather than increasing it.
optionExplanations.E: MDM2 does not primarily suppress BCL2.

questions.takeaway: MDM2 ubiquitinates p53.
questions.recognition: Wild-type TP53 with low p53 protein suggests excessive MDM2 activity.

questions.explanation: Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.

optionExplanations.A: Toxoplasma most classically causes CNS lesions and neurologic findings.
optionExplanations.B: MAC typically appears at more profound immunosuppression and often causes disseminated disease.
optionExplanations.C: Cryptococcus is a classic cause of meningitis in advanced HIV.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pneumocystis pneumonia classically occurs with CD4 counts below 200 and causes subacute fever, dry cough, dyspnea, and diffuse bilateral pulmonary infiltrates.
optionExplanations.E: CMV classically causes retinitis, esophagitis, or colitis at very low CD4 counts.

questions.takeaway: Pneumocystis is the classic pulmonary OI below 200 CD4 cells/µL.
questions.recognition: Use CD4 thresholds as pattern-recognition anchors.

questions.takeaway: AMP activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.
questions.recognition: PFK-1 is the high-yield glycolytic checkpoint for low-energy states.

questions.stem: A receptor has constitutive activity even in the absence of ligand. A new drug binds the receptor and reduces signaling below the basal level. Which term best describes this drug?
questions.hint: The key phrase is “below basal activity.”
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.

optionExplanations.A: A positive allosteric modulator enhances receptor responsiveness.
optionExplanations.B: A partial agonist still increases activity above baseline, though less than a full agonist.
optionExplanations.C: A full agonist increases receptor signaling.
optionExplanations.D: A neutral antagonist blocks agonists but does not reduce constitutive activity.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Inverse agonists preferentially stabilize the inactive receptor state and reduce constitutive signaling below baseline.

questions.takeaway: Inverse agonist = negative efficacy at a constitutively active receptor.
questions.recognition: Constitutive activity plus a drug that lowers the baseline points to an inverse agonist.

questions.stem: A newborn has distal intestinal aganglionosis and fails to pass meconium. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which developmental process failed?
options: Migration of neural crest cells into the hindgut
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.

optionExplanations.A: The notochord organizes axial development but does not directly populate enteric ganglia.
optionExplanations.B: Persistence can produce sacrococcygeal teratoma.
optionExplanations.C: Intermediate mesoderm forms urogenital structures, not enteric neurons.
optionExplanations.D: Failure causes neural-tube defects, not enteric aganglionosis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Hirschsprung disease results from failed neural crest migration into the distal bowel, producing an aganglionic segment that cannot relax normally.

questions.takeaway: Hirschsprung = failed neural crest migration.
questions.recognition: Newborn obstruction + absent ganglion cells is a neural-crest question.

questions.stem: A patient develops urticaria, wheezing, facial swelling, and hypotension within minutes of peanut exposure. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which immune mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.

optionExplanations.A: This is a Type II mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: This is a Type III mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: Complement deficiency predisposes to infection rather than causing this immediate allergic syndrome.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Anaphylaxis is a Type I hypersensitivity reaction. Allergen cross-linking of mast-cell-bound IgE triggers rapid mediator release causing bronchoconstriction, vasodilation, and increased vascular permeability.
optionExplanations.E: This is Type IV hypersensitivity and develops over a longer interval.

questions.takeaway: Type I = IgE + mast cells.
questions.recognition: Rapid hypotension and wheezing after exposure is anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent hemarthroses. PT is normal, aPTT is prolonged and corrects with mixing, and factor VIII activity is markedly reduced. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: Deep bleeding + VIII deficiency = Hemophilia A.
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.

optionExplanations.A: This is a platelet-adhesion defect with giant platelets.
optionExplanations.B: vWD more often causes mucocutaneous bleeding and abnormal platelet adhesion.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hemophilia A is an X-linked factor VIII deficiency causing deep-tissue bleeding and hemarthroses. A simple factor deficiency corrects on mixing study.
optionExplanations.D: Factor XII deficiency can prolong aPTT but usually does not cause clinical bleeding.
optionExplanations.E: Hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency.

questions.takeaway: Hemophilia A = factor VIII deficiency.
questions.recognition: Hemarthroses are a secondary-hemostasis clue.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced illness asks how hospice differs from palliative care. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Hospice requires expected death within 24 hours
Hospice generally serves patients with an estimated prognosis of about 6 months or less
Palliative care cannot be given during chemotherapy
Hospice and palliative care are identical
questions.hint: Hospice is the narrower end-of-life model.
questions.explanation: Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.

optionExplanations.A: Hospice addresses many physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs.
optionExplanations.B: Hospice is not limited to the final day of life.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hospice is a specific end-of-life model generally used when prognosis is approximately 6 months or less and care is focused primarily on comfort.
optionExplanations.D: Palliative care can be concurrent with disease-directed treatment.
optionExplanations.E: Palliative care is broader and can occur much earlier.

questions.takeaway: Hospice is generally associated with a prognosis of about 6 months or less.
questions.recognition: Palliative care is broad; hospice has a more specific end-of-life eligibility framework.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man develops right-sided colon cancer. Several first-degree relatives developed colon or endometrial cancer before age 50, and tumor testing shows microsatellite instability. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which DNA repair system is defective?
questions.hint: Family history + right colon/endometrium + MSI = mismatch repair.
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

optionExplanations.A: NER is associated with bulky DNA lesions and xeroderma pigmentosum.
optionExplanations.B: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks.
optionExplanations.C: BER repairs small altered bases rather than replication mismatches.
optionExplanations.D: This is not the pathway responsible for Lynch syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited defects in mismatch-repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, leading to microsatellite instability.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome = defective DNA mismatch repair.
questions.recognition: Microsatellite instability is the biochemical fingerprint of mismatch-repair failure.

questions.stem: A patient has anemia, jaundice, elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, and reticulocytosis after mechanical heart-valve placement. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which additional finding most strongly supports intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.

optionExplanations.A: Splenomegaly is more strongly associated with chronic extravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: Ferritin is nonspecific and does not directly identify intravascular hemolysis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Free plasma hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis binds and consumes haptoglobin, making a very low or undetectable haptoglobin level a strong clue.
optionExplanations.D: Erythropoietin generally rises in response to anemia.
optionExplanations.E: This can occur in hereditary spherocytosis but is not the best marker of intravascular destruction.

questions.takeaway: Intravascular hemolysis lowers haptoglobin.
questions.recognition: Mechanical hemolysis plus low haptoglobin fits intravascular destruction.

questions.stem: A growth factor binds a receptor tyrosine kinase. GRB2 and SOS activate Ras. Which downstream sequence most directly promotes proliferative gene transcription?
questions.hint: Think of the classic MAPK kinase cascade.
questions.explanation: The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.

optionExplanations.A: Smad signaling is associated with TGF-beta receptors and does not proceed through Gq.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. The canonical mitogenic MAP-kinase cascade downstream of Ras is RAS → RAF → MEK → ERK, which alters transcription and promotes proliferation.
optionExplanations.C: This is a GPCR pathway.
optionExplanations.D: JAK/STAT is a cytokine-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.E: PI3K signals mainly through PIP3 and AKT, not caspase-8.

questions.takeaway: RTK/GRB2/SOS → Ras → Raf → MEK → ERK.
questions.recognition: A Ras question usually wants the MAPK cascade.

questions.stem: A renal artery thrombosis causes an infarct. Days later, dead renal tubules retain their general architectural outlines despite loss of nuclei. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which pattern of necrosis is present?
questions.hint: Most solid-organ infarcts coagulate; brain liquefies.
questions.explanation: Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.

optionExplanations.A: Caseous necrosis is classically associated with tuberculosis.
optionExplanations.B: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in damaged vessel walls, such as vasculitis.
optionExplanations.C: Fat necrosis occurs in settings such as acute pancreatitis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Ischemic injury in most solid organs causes coagulative necrosis, in which protein denaturation preserves tissue architecture temporarily. The major ischemic exception is the brain.
optionExplanations.E: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain infarction and many abscesses.

questions.takeaway: Coagulative necrosis preserves tissue architecture for a time.
questions.recognition: Kidney/heart/spleen infarct = coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: A patient develops an intensely pruritic rash 48 hours after nickel exposure. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Contact dermatitis is a Type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized T cells rather than antibodies.
optionExplanations.B: Complement deficiency does not produce contact dermatitis.
optionExplanations.C: Type I reactions are immediate rather than delayed by 48 hours.
optionExplanations.D: Type III involves soluble immune complexes.
optionExplanations.E: Type II targets fixed antigens with IgG/IgM.

questions.takeaway: Type IV = delayed, T-cell mediated.
questions.recognition: Nickel and poison ivy are classic Type IV triggers.

questions.stem: A patient with MRSA bacteremia receives vancomycin. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which bacterial structure does the drug bind?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.

optionExplanations.A: This is inhibited by trimethoprim.
optionExplanations.B: This is inhibited by rifampin.
optionExplanations.C: This is targeted by aminoglycosides and tetracyclines.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini of peptidoglycan precursors and blocks cell-wall polymerization. It does not bind PBPs directly.
optionExplanations.E: This is targeted by fluoroquinolones.

questions.takeaway: Vancomycin binds D-Ala-D-Ala.
questions.recognition: Differentiate vancomycin from beta-lactams: substrate binding versus PBP binding.

questions.stem: An infant has severe fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia, and marked hepatomegaly. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Severe fasting hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + hepatomegaly = GSD I.
questions.explanation: Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Deficiency causes McArdle disease with exercise intolerance.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Von Gierke disease results from glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency, preventing release of free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.C: Deficiency causes Andersen disease with abnormal glycogen and cirrhosis.
optionExplanations.D: Deficiency causes Pompe disease with cardiomyopathy and hypotonia.
optionExplanations.E: Deficiency causes Cori disease, which is generally milder and preserves gluconeogenesis.

questions.takeaway: Von Gierke = glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency.
questions.recognition: If both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis fail at the final step, think G6Pase.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman develops sudden severe abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, and a tender firm uterus. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or hypertonicity.
optionExplanations.B: A partial mole is a triploid abnormal gestation and does not fit this late-pregnancy emergency.
optionExplanations.C: Previa typically causes painless bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Accreta presents mainly as abnormal placental adherence and postpartum hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.E: Cervical insufficiency usually causes painless dilation in the second trimester.

questions.takeaway: Abruption causes painful bleeding and a tender/firm uterus.
questions.recognition: Pain + bleeding + firm uterus is a classic triad.

questions.stem: A patient develops jaundice and dark urine after an oxidant drug. Smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.

optionExplanations.A: This causes DAT-positive spherocytic hemolysis.
optionExplanations.B: This causes spherocytes due to membrane-skeleton defects.
optionExplanations.C: This causes microcytosis from reduced beta-globin synthesis.
optionExplanations.D: This causes microcytic anemia without oxidant-triggered hemolysis.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. G6PD deficiency reduces NADPH and reduced glutathione, so oxidant stress denatures hemoglobin into Heinz bodies. Splenic removal of Heinz-body-containing membrane produces bite cells.

questions.takeaway: G6PD deficiency causes episodic oxidative hemolysis.
questions.recognition: Bite cells are a classic post-Heinz-body clue.

questions.stem: An older adult has large tense blisters. Biopsy shows the entire epidermis separating from the underlying basement membrane while epidermal cells remain attached to one another. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which structure is targeted?
questions.explanation: Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.

optionExplanations.A: Tight junctions regulate paracellular permeability.
optionExplanations.B: Desmosomal disruption produces intraepidermal acantholysis and flaccid blisters.
optionExplanations.C: Gap junctions mediate cell communication.
optionExplanations.D: Adherens junctions link actin cytoskeletons between cells.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Bullous pemphigoid involves autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins at the dermal-epidermal junction, producing subepidermal separation and tense blisters.

questions.takeaway: Bullous pemphigoid targets hemidesmosomes.
questions.recognition: Flaccid = desmosomes; tense = hemidesmosomes.

questions.stem: A child has impaired phagocytosis of encapsulated bacteria because the organisms are not efficiently coated for complement-receptor recognition. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which complement component normally performs this function?
questions.explanation: C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. C3b is the major complement opsonin. It coats microbial surfaces and binds complement receptors on phagocytes, greatly improving engulfment of encapsulated bacteria.
optionExplanations.B: C5a is a potent chemotactic and inflammatory mediator.
optionExplanations.C: C9 participates in the membrane attack complex.
optionExplanations.D: C1 inhibitor regulates complement/contact activation rather than opsonizing microbes.
optionExplanations.E: C3a is mainly an anaphylatoxin.

questions.takeaway: C3b coats; C3a/C5a inflame; C5b-9 punches holes.
questions.recognition: Encapsulated organism + complement receptor = C3b.

questions.stem: Severe DNA damage triggers mitochondrial outer-membrane permeabilization and cytochrome-c release. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which initiator caspase is activated downstream?
questions.explanation: Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.

optionExplanations.A: Caspase-8 is the classic initiator of the extrinsic death-receptor pathway.
optionExplanations.B: Caspase-1 is associated with inflammasome signaling.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Cytochrome c forms the apoptosome and activates caspase-9, which then activates executioner caspases such as caspase-3.
optionExplanations.D: Caspase-3 is an executioner caspase, not the primary intrinsic initiator.
optionExplanations.E: This is not the principal initiator of mitochondrial apoptosis.

questions.takeaway: Intrinsic apoptosis activates caspase-9; extrinsic activates caspase-8.
questions.recognition: Cytochrome c release should trigger caspase-9.

questions.stem: A sperm penetrates the zona pellucida and fuses with the oocyte membrane. Cortical granules are released immediately afterward. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What is the main purpose of the cortical reaction?
questions.hint: One sperm in; lock the door.
questions.explanation: The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.

optionExplanations.A: Pronuclear formation occurs later and is not the primary effect of cortical granule release.
optionExplanations.B: Cleavage follows fertilization but is not the purpose of the cortical reaction.
optionExplanations.C: Capacitation occurs before the sperm reaches and fuses with the oocyte.
optionExplanations.D: Trophoblast differentiation occurs during later blastocyst development.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The cortical reaction modifies the zona pellucida after sperm-oocyte fusion so additional sperm cannot bind and penetrate, preventing polyspermy.

questions.takeaway: Cortical reaction = block to polyspermy.
questions.recognition: Cortical granules are a post-fusion anti-polyspermy mechanism.

questions.stem: A cancer-screening program detects tumors several years earlier. Five-year survival after diagnosis increases, but cancer-specific mortality is unchanged. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which bias best explains the apparent benefit?
questions.hint: Earlier diagnosis without later death = lead-time bias.
questions.explanation: Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.

optionExplanations.A: Observer bias arises from measurement influenced by expectations.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Lead-time bias occurs when screening moves the diagnosis earlier without changing the time of death. Measured survival from diagnosis becomes longer even though mortality is unchanged.
optionExplanations.C: Selection bias concerns who enters or remains in a study.
optionExplanations.D: Recall bias affects remembered exposures.
optionExplanations.E: Length-time bias preferentially detects slower-growing disease.

questions.takeaway: Lead-time bias inflates post-diagnosis survival without improving mortality.
questions.recognition: Always compare survival to disease-specific mortality in screening questions.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man receives a drug by continuous IV infusion. Renal function improves and the drug clearance doubles while the desired steady-state concentration remains unchanged. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What dosing change is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Maintenance dosing rate is proportional to clearance times the target concentration. If clearance doubles and the target concentration is unchanged, the maintenance rate must increase.
optionExplanations.B: Higher clearance lowers steady-state concentration unless dosing rate is increased.
optionExplanations.C: Volume of distribution is not a dosing adjustment.
optionExplanations.D: Lowering the rate would further reduce steady-state exposure.
optionExplanations.E: Loading dose depends mainly on volume of distribution and target concentration, not clearance.

questions.takeaway: Maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.
questions.recognition: When clearance changes, maintenance dosing changes; loading dose is tied to Vd.

questions.stem: A patient with candidemia receives micafungin. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which fungal structure is most directly disrupted?
options: Beta-1,3-D-glucan component of the fungal cell wall
Ergosterol in the membrane through pore formation
questions.explanation: Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.

optionExplanations.A: Flucytosine metabolites interfere with nucleic-acid synthesis, not beta-glucan.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Echinocandins such as micafungin inhibit beta-1,3-D-glucan synthase, weakening the fungal cell wall.
optionExplanations.C: Azoles inhibit this enzyme and reduce ergosterol synthesis.
optionExplanations.D: Terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase.
optionExplanations.E: Polyenes bind ergosterol and form pores.

questions.takeaway: Micafungin inhibits beta-1,3-D-glucan synthesis.
questions.recognition: Candida + micafungin should trigger echinocandin cell-wall inhibition.

questions.stem: A young child has severe microcytic anemia, marrow expansion, skeletal changes, hepatosplenomegaly, and transfusion dependence. Hemoglobin analysis shows very high HbF and almost no HbA. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: High HbF + absent HbA + severe childhood disease = beta-thal major.
questions.explanation: Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.

optionExplanations.A: HbC trait is generally mild.
optionExplanations.B: Sickle trait has HbA greater than HbS and is usually asymptomatic.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Severe beta-globin deficiency produces beta-thalassemia major. Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and HbF becomes markedly elevated because normal HbA cannot be produced adequately.
optionExplanations.D: Iron deficiency does not produce this hemoglobin pattern or marrow-expansion syndrome.
optionExplanations.E: Alpha trait is generally mild microcytosis.

questions.takeaway: Beta-thalassemia major causes severe ineffective erythropoiesis.
questions.recognition: Think of globin composition, not just microcytosis.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic back pain says, “My spine must be getting destroyed. It will only get worse, and there is nothing I can do.” The patient spends hours ruminating about the pain. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which psychological construct is most strongly demonstrated?
questions.explanation: Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.

optionExplanations.A: Values-based action involves pursuing meaningful activities despite symptoms.
optionExplanations.B: Self-efficacy is confidence in one’s ability to function despite pain.
optionExplanations.C: Pacing is structured activity management.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Pain catastrophizing consists of rumination, magnification of threat, and helplessness. It is associated with worse pain-related disability and distress.
optionExplanations.E: Acceptance is adaptive willingness to experience pain while functioning.

questions.takeaway: Catastrophizing = rumination + magnification + helplessness.
questions.recognition: “It is terrible and I cannot cope” is the core cognitive pattern.

questions.stem: A breast-fed infant develops vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly, failure to thrive, and cataracts. Urine contains a reducing sugar but the glucose dipstick is negative. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Milk exposure + cataracts + liver disease = classic galactosemia.
questions.explanation: Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.

optionExplanations.A: This causes von Gierke disease rather than a milk-triggered galactose syndrome.
optionExplanations.B: Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance after fruit/sucrose exposure.
optionExplanations.C: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign fructosuria.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Classic galactosemia results from GALT deficiency, causing toxic galactose-1-phosphate accumulation, liver disease, failure to thrive, and cataracts after lactose-containing milk exposure.
optionExplanations.E: Galactokinase deficiency is milder and mainly causes cataracts without severe hepatic disease.

questions.takeaway: Classic galactosemia = GALT deficiency.
questions.recognition: If cataracts are accompanied by severe systemic toxicity, distinguish GALT deficiency from isolated galactokinase deficiency.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman receives a reversible antagonist with an agonist. The agonist dose-response curve shifts to the right, but a sufficiently high agonist dose still reaches the original maximum response. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What type of antagonist was given?
questions.explanation: A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.

optionExplanations.A: A partial agonist activates the receptor but has lower efficacy.
optionExplanations.B: Irreversible blockade generally cannot be fully overcome and can reduce Emax.
optionExplanations.C: An inverse agonist reduces constitutive receptor signaling below baseline.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A reversible competitive antagonist increases the agonist concentration needed for a given effect but can be surmounted by enough agonist. Thus potency falls while Emax is preserved.
optionExplanations.E: Noncompetitive antagonism typically decreases maximal efficacy.

questions.takeaway: Competitive antagonism decreases apparent potency without decreasing maximal efficacy.
questions.recognition: If the maximum is preserved, think surmountable competitive antagonism.

questions.stem: A patient begins an HIV integrase strand-transfer inhibitor. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which stage of viral replication is directly inhibited?
options: Reverse transcription of RNA into DNA
Insertion of viral DNA into the host genome
questions.hint: Integrase does exactly what its name suggests.
questions.explanation: Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.

optionExplanations.A: Protease inhibitors block maturation.
optionExplanations.B: Integrase inhibitors act before productive proviral transcription and budding.
optionExplanations.C: NRTIs and NNRTIs inhibit reverse transcription.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Integrase inhibitors prevent incorporation of newly synthesized HIV DNA into host chromosomal DNA, blocking formation of a functional provirus.
optionExplanations.E: This is an earlier entry step.

questions.takeaway: INSTIs block integration of viral DNA into host DNA.
questions.recognition: HIV drug-class questions often map directly to the viral life cycle.

questions.stem: A prosthetic-joint infection grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative gram-positive cocci that are sensitive to novobiocin. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which organism is most likely?
questions.hint: Device infection + coag negative + novobiocin sensitive = epidermidis.
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.

optionExplanations.A: This organism is catalase negative.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Staphylococcus epidermidis is coagulase negative, novobiocin sensitive, and strongly associated with prosthetic devices and biofilms.
optionExplanations.C: Enterococcus is catalase negative and is identified by other biochemical features.
optionExplanations.D: S aureus is coagulase positive.
optionExplanations.E: S saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and classically associated with UTIs.

questions.takeaway: S epidermidis is the prosthetic-device staphylococcus.
questions.recognition: Novobiocin sensitivity distinguishes it from S saprophyticus.

questions.stem: A pesticide prevents electrons from NADH from entering the mitochondrial respiratory chain by blocking Complex I. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which compound has this effect?
questions.hint: Map each classic toxin to its ETC target.
questions.explanation: Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.

optionExplanations.A: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase.
optionExplanations.B: 2,4-DNP uncouples oxidative phosphorylation rather than blocking Complex I.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Rotenone inhibits electron-transport-chain Complex I, preventing transfer of electrons from NADH to coenzyme Q.
optionExplanations.D: Antimycin A inhibits Complex III.
optionExplanations.E: Cyanide inhibits Complex IV.

questions.takeaway: Rotenone = Complex I; antimycin = III; cyanide = IV; oligomycin = ATP synthase.
questions.recognition: Complex I blocker is rotenone.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a persistent firm 3-cm palpable breast mass and has never undergone breast imaging. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which initial imaging study is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.

optionExplanations.A: PET is not the first-line evaluation of a localized new breast mass.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. For a patient younger than 30 with a palpable breast mass, ultrasound is generally the preferred initial imaging modality because younger breasts are denser and ultrasound can characterize solid versus cystic lesions.
optionExplanations.C: A persistent firm mass requires evaluation.
optionExplanations.D: CT does not replace dedicated breast imaging.
optionExplanations.E: MRI has selected indications but is not the usual first study for a palpable mass in a patient under 30.

questions.takeaway: Under 30 with a palpable mass → ultrasound first.
questions.recognition: Do not jump to mammography/PET in a young patient with a new mass.

questions.stem: A young woman has recurrent epistaxis, easy bruising, and menorrhagia. Platelet count and PT are normal, and ristocetin-dependent activity is decreased. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.

optionExplanations.A: ITP causes thrombocytopenia, whereas this platelet count is normal.
optionExplanations.B: Factor V Leiden is a thrombophilia, not a bleeding disorder.
optionExplanations.C: Hemophilia causes deep tissue bleeding and hemarthroses rather than predominantly mucosal bleeding.
optionExplanations.D: Glanzmann causes defective aggregation but preserves ristocetin-dependent adhesion.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. von Willebrand disease impairs GpIb-mediated platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. The clinical pattern is mucocutaneous bleeding with abnormal ristocetin testing.

questions.takeaway: vWF mediates platelet adhesion and stabilizes factor VIII.
questions.recognition: Menorrhagia and epistaxis point toward primary hemostasis.

questions.stem: A tumor overexpresses cyclin D1, increasing cyclin D-CDK4/6 activity. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which molecular event most directly promotes entry into S phase?
options: Phosphorylation of RB with release of E2F
questions.hint: RB is the brake; phosphorylation releases E2F.
questions.explanation: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.

optionExplanations.A: p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases and promotes arrest.
optionExplanations.B: Hypophosphorylated RB binds and restrains E2F.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB. Phosphorylated RB releases E2F, allowing transcription of genes required for DNA synthesis and S-phase entry.
optionExplanations.D: This would block rather than promote S-phase progression.
optionExplanations.E: Loss of E2F would reduce S-phase gene transcription.

questions.takeaway: Cyclin D/CDK4/6 → pRB → free E2F → S phase.
questions.recognition: Cyclin D questions usually converge on RB phosphorylation.

questions.stem: A developmental defect disrupts formation of somites, producing abnormalities of vertebrae, skeletal muscle, and dermis. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which embryologic tissue was affected?
questions.hint: Somites sit beside the neural tube.
questions.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, whose subdivisions contribute to vertebrae/ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis.
optionExplanations.B: Endoderm forms many internal epithelial linings.
optionExplanations.C: Neural crest forms PNS structures, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, and craniofacial tissues.
optionExplanations.D: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body-wall, cardiovascular, and visceral structures.
optionExplanations.E: Intermediate mesoderm contributes to kidneys, gonads, and genital ducts.

questions.takeaway: Paraxial mesoderm → somites.
questions.recognition: Vertebrae + muscle + dermis in one stem = somites.

questions.stem: An autosomal recessive disease occurs in 1 of every 2,500 individuals in a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. What is the mutant allele frequency q?
questions.explanation: For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. For an autosomal recessive disease, q² equals prevalence. The square root of 1/2500 is 1/50.
optionExplanations.B: This is not the square root of the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.C: That would correspond to q² of 1/10,000.
optionExplanations.D: That is q², the disease prevalence.
optionExplanations.E: That would produce a substantially higher disease prevalence.

questions.takeaway: Hardy-Weinberg: p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
questions.recognition: Take the square root before calculating carrier frequency.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell phagocytoses an extracellular bacterial protein and processes it in an endosomal compartment. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which molecule presents the peptide to helper T cells?
questions.explanation: Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.

optionExplanations.A: CD8 is a T-cell coreceptor, not the presenting molecule.
optionExplanations.B: Fc receptors facilitate uptake/activation but are not the peptide-presenting molecule to helper T cells.
optionExplanations.C: Beta-2 microglobulin is a component of MHC I and does not independently present peptide.
optionExplanations.D: MHC I usually presents endogenous intracellular peptides to CD8 T cells.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Exogenous antigens taken up by professional antigen-presenting cells are processed in endosomes/lysosomes and loaded onto MHC class II for recognition by CD4 T cells.

questions.takeaway: Exogenous antigen → MHC II → CD4.
questions.recognition: Phagocytosed extracellular protein is a classic MHC II setup.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic patient has an automated platelet count of 35,000/µL, but the peripheral smear shows numerous platelet clumps. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Repeat the platelet count with a fresh specimen and evaluate for laboratory artifact
questions.hint: Always inspect the smear before treating the number.
questions.explanation: Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.

optionExplanations.A: Do not diagnose immune thrombocytopenia before confirming that the low count is real.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Platelet clumping can cause pseudothrombocytopenia on automated analyzers. A repeat count using a fresh sample or different anticoagulant confirms whether thrombocytopenia is genuine.
optionExplanations.C: An asymptomatic patient with obvious clumping may not truly be thrombocytopenic.
optionExplanations.D: This is unnecessarily invasive before excluding pseudothrombocytopenia.
optionExplanations.E: Plasma exchange is used in TTP, which would require a different clinical picture.

questions.takeaway: Platelet clumping can falsely lower the automated count.
questions.recognition: Asymptomatic + clumps = pseudothrombocytopenia until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: During prolonged fasting, beta-oxidation raises mitochondrial acetyl-CoA. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which enzyme is directly activated by acetyl-CoA?
questions.hint: High acetyl-CoA tells the liver to spare pyruvate for glucose production.
questions.explanation: Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.

optionExplanations.A: Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme and is inhibited during hepatic fasting.
optionExplanations.B: This enzyme is regulated mainly by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate rather than direct acetyl-CoA activation.
optionExplanations.C: PFK-1 controls glycolysis and is not activated by acetyl-CoA.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Acetyl-CoA allosterically activates mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase, directing pyruvate toward oxaloacetate and gluconeogenesis during fasting.
optionExplanations.E: Hexokinase is not directly activated by acetyl-CoA.

questions.takeaway: Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase.
questions.recognition: Fasting + acetyl-CoA + gluconeogenesis = pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: A woman has endometrial cancer and a strong family history of early-onset colorectal cancer. Her tumor shows loss of MSH2 and MSH6 expression. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which hereditary syndrome is most likely?
questions.explanation: Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.

optionExplanations.A: This is caused by RB1 loss.
optionExplanations.B: FAP is caused by APC mutations and usually causes hundreds to thousands of adenomas.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Lynch syndrome is caused by inherited mismatch-repair defects and is associated with colorectal and endometrial cancers, often with relatively few polyps.
optionExplanations.D: Li-Fraumeni is due to germline TP53 mutations and a different tumor spectrum.
optionExplanations.E: MEN2 is due to activating RET mutations.

questions.takeaway: Lynch syndrome is a mismatch-repair cancer syndrome.
questions.recognition: MSH2/MSH6 loss is a strong clue for Lynch syndrome.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man has a hormone that binds a Gs-coupled receptor on target cells. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which intracellular change occurs first downstream of the activated G alpha subunit?
options: Activation of phospholipase C and increased IP3/DAG
Activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased cAMP
Activation of receptor tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation
questions.explanation: Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.

optionExplanations.A: This is the classic Gq pathway.
optionExplanations.B: JAK/STAT is used by cytokine receptors rather than classical Gs-coupled GPCRs.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Gs activates adenylyl cyclase, increasing cAMP and downstream protein kinase A activity.
optionExplanations.D: That belongs to RTK signaling, not Gs GPCR signaling.
optionExplanations.E: This is the classic Gi effect.

questions.takeaway: Gs → adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → PKA.
questions.recognition: The letter “s” in Gs can be remembered as “stimulates” adenylyl cyclase.

questions.stem: A bacterial pneumonia is treated with a beta-lactam antibiotic that covalently binds penicillin-binding proteins. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which process is directly inhibited?
questions.explanation: Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: Fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase.
optionExplanations.B: Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines target the 30S subunit.
optionExplanations.C: Sulfonamides and trimethoprim inhibit folate pathways.
optionExplanations.D: Rifamycins inhibit bacterial RNA polymerase.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Beta-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins, including transpeptidases, and prevent normal peptidoglycan cross-linking in actively growing bacteria.

questions.takeaway: Beta-lactams inhibit peptidoglycan cross-linking.
questions.recognition: Cell-wall question + PBP should be automatic.

questions.stem: A patient has mucosal bleeding. Platelet count is normal. Aggregation is impaired with most agonists, but ristocetin response is preserved. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which receptor is defective?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is caused by GpIIb/IIIa deficiency, preventing fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation. vWF-GpIb adhesion remains intact, so ristocetin testing is normal.
optionExplanations.B: Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia A with deep tissue bleeding.
optionExplanations.C: P2Y12 participates in ADP-mediated platelet activation but does not produce the classic pattern described.
optionExplanations.D: Thrombomodulin participates in the protein C anticoagulant pathway.
optionExplanations.E: GpIb deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome and abnormal ristocetin response.

questions.takeaway: Glanzmann = GpIIb/IIIa aggregation defect.
questions.recognition: Differentiate Glanzmann from Bernard-Soulier using ristocetin.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman in the third trimester has sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding without uterine tenderness. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: This usually causes fever and uterine tenderness.
optionExplanations.B: Abruption usually causes painful bleeding and a tender, firm uterus.
optionExplanations.C: Molar pregnancy typically presents earlier with abnormal trophoblastic findings.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Placenta previa occurs when placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os and classically causes painless third-trimester bleeding.
optionExplanations.E: Accreta causes abnormal adherence and postpartum hemorrhage rather than classic painless antepartum bleeding.

questions.takeaway: Previa is painless; abruption is painful.
questions.recognition: The pain distinction is the fastest way to separate previa from abruption.

questions.stem: A child has extreme photosensitivity and develops multiple skin cancers on sun-exposed areas. Cells cannot appropriately remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which DNA repair pathway is defective?
questions.explanation: Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.

optionExplanations.A: MMR corrects replication mismatches and insertion-deletion loops.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Xeroderma pigmentosum results from defective nucleotide excision repair, which normally removes bulky helix-distorting lesions such as UV-induced pyrimidine dimers.
optionExplanations.C: BER repairs small, non-helix-distorting base lesions.
optionExplanations.D: NHEJ repairs double-strand breaks without a homologous template.
optionExplanations.E: HR repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous template.

questions.takeaway: NER removes bulky helix-distorting DNA lesions.
questions.recognition: UV sensitivity plus early skin cancers should trigger xeroderma pigmentosum and NER.

questions.stem: A patient receives a foreign protein. One week later, fever, urticaria, arthralgias, proteinuria, and low complement develop. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which mechanism is responsible?
questions.hint: Immune complexes + low complement = Type III.
questions.explanation: Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Serum sickness is a Type III hypersensitivity reaction in which soluble antigen-antibody complexes form, deposit in tissues, activate complement, and trigger inflammation.
optionExplanations.B: Loss of tolerance may cause autoimmunity but does not describe this immune-complex effector mechanism.
optionExplanations.C: Type I is immediate and IgE mediated.
optionExplanations.D: Type II targets fixed cell-surface/tissue antigens.
optionExplanations.E: Type IV is T-cell mediated.

questions.takeaway: Type III = circulating immune-complex deposition.
questions.recognition: Fever + rash + arthralgia after foreign protein is serum sickness.

questions.stem: A patient with metastatic cancer is still receiving chemotherapy but has severe pain, nausea, anxiety, and difficulty discussing future goals. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which statement about palliative care is most accurate?
options: It requires a prognosis under 6 months
It is appropriate only after cancer therapy stops
It is limited to opioid management
It can be provided concurrently with disease-directed therapy
questions.hint: Do not equate palliative care with hospice.
questions.explanation: Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.

optionExplanations.A: That criterion is more characteristic of hospice eligibility.
optionExplanations.B: Palliative care can begin early and coexist with treatment.
optionExplanations.C: Hospice is a narrower end-of-life model within the broader palliative approach.
optionExplanations.D: Palliative care addresses symptoms, communication, psychosocial support, and goals of care.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Palliative care can be integrated at any stage of serious illness and may be delivered alongside chemotherapy, radiation, surgery, or other disease-directed treatment.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care can be concurrent with active treatment.
questions.recognition: If the stem says “still receiving treatment,” palliative care can still be appropriate.

questions.stem: An infant develops vomiting, sweating, profound hypoglycemia, and hepatomegaly shortly after fruit juice is introduced. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.hint: Symptoms begin when fructose/sucrose enters the diet.
questions.explanation: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

optionExplanations.A: Galactokinase deficiency primarily causes cataracts.
optionExplanations.B: Fructokinase deficiency causes benign essential fructosuria.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by aldolase B deficiency. Fructose-1-phosphate accumulates, trapping phosphate and impairing glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
optionExplanations.D: This causes von Gierke disease and is not specifically triggered by fructose introduction.
optionExplanations.E: GALT deficiency causes classic galactosemia after milk exposure.

questions.takeaway: Hereditary fructose intolerance = aldolase B deficiency.
questions.recognition: Fruit introduction + hypoglycemia + liver dysfunction is the classic pattern.

questions.stem: A child with chronic hemolytic anemia has deletion of three alpha-globin genes. The finding is confirmed on repeat testing. Which abnormal hemoglobin is expected?
options: Hb Barts composed of gamma4 tetramers
