optionExplanations.D: These do not explain calcium-mediated membrane and cytoskeletal destruction.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Elevated cytosolic calcium activates phospholipases that damage membranes and proteases that degrade cytoskeletal and structural proteins. Calcium also worsens mitochondrial dysfunction.

questions.takeaway: Calcium activates phospholipases, proteases, endonucleases, and ATPases.
questions.recognition: In ischemic injury, calcium is dangerous because it activates degradative enzymes.

questions.stem: A healthy sperm reaches the secondary oocyte under normal physiologic conditions. The clinician reviews the underlying mechanism with the patient. Where does fertilization most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Human fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube. The resulting zygote then undergoes cleavage while traveling toward the uterine cavity.
optionExplanations.B: The cervix is part of the sperm’s route but not the usual fertilization site.
optionExplanations.C: The blastocyst later implants in the uterus; fertilization usually occurs before arrival there.
optionExplanations.D: The ampulla, not the isthmus, is the most common site.
optionExplanations.E: The oocyte is released from the ovary before fertilization.

questions.takeaway: Fertilization = ampulla; implantation = endometrium.
questions.recognition: Ampulla is the classic normal fertilization site.

questions.stem: A healthy sperm fertilizes a secondary oocyte at the most common physiologic site. Where does fertilization occur?
questions.hint: Separate the site of fertilization from the later site of implantation.
questions.explanation: Human fertilization normally occurs within the ampulla of the uterine tube. The newly formed zygote subsequently undergoes cleavage as it travels toward the uterine cavity.

optionExplanations.A: The cervix is part of the route sperm travel through, but it is not the normal site of fertilization.
optionExplanations.B: The uterine cavity is where the blastocyst later implants; fertilization normally occurs before the conceptus reaches the uterus.
optionExplanations.C: The ovary releases the oocyte, but sperm-oocyte fusion normally occurs after the oocyte enters the uterine tube.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The ampulla is the widest portion of the uterine tube and the most common site of fertilization.
optionExplanations.E: Sperm may be deposited in the vagina, but fertilization normally occurs much farther proximally.

questions.takeaway: Fertilization = ampulla. Implantation = endometrium several days later.
questions.recognition: When a Step 1 question asks for the normal site of fertilization, choose the ampulla of the uterine tube.

questions.stem: A normal conceptus has progressed through cleavage and morula formation and has developed into a blastocyst. At approximately what time does implantation normally begin?
options: At the end of the embryonic period
questions.hint: Think in days, not weeks. Implantation starts shortly after blastocyst formation.
questions.explanation: The early developmental sequence is fertilization → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → implantation. Blastocyst formation occurs around days 4–5, and implantation begins approximately days 5–7 after fertilization.

optionExplanations.A: Several hours is too early; cleavage and blastocyst formation must occur first.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Implantation begins approximately days 5–7 after fertilization.
optionExplanations.C: The embryonic period extends through week 8; implantation occurs much earlier.
optionExplanations.D: Week 5 is far too late for normal implantation.
optionExplanations.E: Placental and fetal circulation develop after implantation has already begun.

questions.takeaway: Blastocyst by about day 5; implantation begins about days 5–7.
questions.recognition: If the stem has already reached the blastocyst stage, implantation is only days away—not weeks.

questions.stem: During gastrulation, cells migrate through the primitive streak to establish the three primary germ layers. Which preexisting cell population gives rise to all three layers of the embryo proper?
questions.hint: The embryo proper comes from the upper layer of the bilaminar disc.
questions.explanation: Cells of the epiblast ultimately generate ectoderm, intraembryonic mesoderm, and definitive endoderm during gastrulation. The hypoblast contributes mainly to extraembryonic endoderm rather than the embryo proper.

optionExplanations.A: The hypoblast contributes primarily to extraembryonic endoderm, including yolk-sac lining.
optionExplanations.B: The cytotrophoblast is a trophoblastic placental cell layer, not the source of the three embryonic germ layers.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The epiblast produces ectoderm, mesoderm, and definitive endoderm.
optionExplanations.D: The syncytiotrophoblast is involved in implantation and placental development.
optionExplanations.E: Extraembryonic mesoderm contributes to extraembryonic support structures rather than all three layers of the embryo proper.

questions.takeaway: All three primary germ layers of the embryo proper arise from epiblast.
questions.recognition: Primitive streak + gastrulation + all three germ layers = epiblast.

questions.stem: A developmental defect disrupts formation of somites. The child subsequently has abnormalities of vertebrae, skeletal muscle, and dermis. Which embryonic tissue was primarily affected?
questions.hint: Somites are segmented blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube.
questions.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm forms somites, which subdivide into structures that contribute to vertebrae and ribs, skeletal muscle, and dermis. Intermediate mesoderm instead contributes prominently to the urogenital system.

optionExplanations.A: Intermediate mesoderm gives rise to much of the kidneys, gonads, and genital ducts.
optionExplanations.B: Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to body wall, serosa, cardiovascular structures, and visceral connective tissues.
optionExplanations.C: Endoderm forms epithelial linings of many internal organs.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms somites and their sclerotome, myotome, and dermatome derivatives.
optionExplanations.E: Neural crest forms many peripheral nervous system, pigment, adrenal-medullary, and craniofacial derivatives.

questions.takeaway: Somites come from paraxial mesoderm.
questions.recognition: Vertebrae + skeletal muscle + dermis in one developmental stem strongly points to somites/paraxial mesoderm.

questions.stem: A congenital malformation selectively affects endodermal derivatives. Which structure is most likely involved?
options: Epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract
questions.hint: Think epithelial linings of internal tubes and glandular parenchyma.
questions.explanation: Endoderm gives rise to the epithelial lining of the gut tube and the epithelial or glandular parenchyma of multiple organs, including the respiratory tract, liver, pancreas, thyroid, thymus, and much of the bladder epithelium.

optionExplanations.A: The epidermis derives from surface ectoderm.
optionExplanations.B: Skeletal muscle derives from paraxial mesoderm.
optionExplanations.C: Vertebral bodies derive from sclerotome of paraxial mesoderm.
optionExplanations.D: The adrenal medulla derives from neural crest.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The epithelial lining of the gastrointestinal tract is a classic endodermal derivative.

questions.takeaway: Endoderm primarily forms internal epithelial linings and glandular parenchyma.
questions.recognition: When the answer choices mix germ-layer derivatives, GI epithelium is the classic endoderm pick.

questions.stem: A woman at 33 weeks' gestation presents with sudden painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. She has no abdominal tenderness or uterine contractions. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: The key contrast is painless versus painful third-trimester bleeding.
questions.explanation: Placenta previa classically presents with painless bleeding in later pregnancy because placental tissue overlies or approaches the internal cervical os. This sharply contrasts with placental abruption, which is classically abrupt and painful.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Painless third-trimester bleeding strongly suggests placenta previa.
optionExplanations.B: Placental abruption usually causes painful bleeding with uterine tenderness or a firm uterus.
optionExplanations.C: Placenta percreta refers to abnormally deep placental invasion through the uterine wall, not the classic painless-bleeding presentation.
optionExplanations.D: Chorioamnionitis typically causes fever, maternal/fetal tachycardia, uterine tenderness, and infectious findings.
optionExplanations.E: Hydatidiform mole presents much earlier and is associated with abnormal trophoblastic proliferation and markedly elevated hCG.

questions.takeaway: Placenta previa = painless late-pregnancy bleeding. Abruption = painful bleeding.
questions.recognition: Bright-red painless bleeding in the third trimester is the classic placenta previa clue.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation develops sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding. The uterus is tender and firm. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.hint: Pain + bleeding + a tender, firm uterus should immediately narrow the differential.
questions.explanation: Placental abruption is premature separation of a normally implanted placenta and classically produces painful vaginal bleeding, abdominal or uterine pain, and uterine tenderness. Placenta previa typically causes painless bleeding.

optionExplanations.A: Placenta previa usually causes painless bleeding and a nontender uterus.
optionExplanations.B: A partial mole is an abnormal triploid gestation and does not present as this late-pregnancy emergency.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Painful bleeding with uterine tenderness and firmness is classic for placental abruption.
optionExplanations.D: Placenta accreta is abnormal placental adherence or invasion and is especially associated with failure of placental separation and postpartum hemorrhage.
optionExplanations.E: Cervical insufficiency is typically painless cervical dilation in the second trimester.

questions.takeaway: Abruption = painful bleeding + tender or firm uterus.
questions.recognition: The painful-versus-painless distinction is one of the fastest ways to separate abruption from previa.

questions.stem: A researcher characterizes leukocytes within healthy decidual tissue in early pregnancy. Which population is most abundant?
questions.hint: The dominant decidual immune cell is an innate lymphocyte with specialized pregnancy functions.
questions.explanation: Uterine or decidual natural killer cells are the dominant local immune population in healthy early pregnancy. These NK cells have specialized roles in trophoblast interaction, vascular remodeling, and placental development rather than functioning simply as conventional cytotoxic NK cells.

optionExplanations.A: B cells are present but are not the dominant decidual leukocyte population.
optionExplanations.B: Eosinophils are not the major normal decidual immune population.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Uterine NK cells make up the largest proportion of leukocytes in healthy decidual tissue.
optionExplanations.D: Plasma cells are not the predominant normal decidual leukocyte population.
optionExplanations.E: Neutrophils are important in acute inflammation but are not the dominant population in healthy decidua.

questions.takeaway: Healthy decidua is rich in specialized uterine NK cells.
questions.recognition: Placental/decidual immune-cell abundance questions usually point to NK cells.

questions.stem: A researcher inhibits indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 at the maternal-fetal interface. Which substance is normally metabolized by this enzyme as part of the tolerance pathway?
questions.hint: IDO1 acts on an essential amino acid involved in immune regulation.
questions.explanation: Indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 metabolizes L-tryptophan and contributes to maternal-fetal immune tolerance and successful trophoblast invasion. Alteration of this pathway can disrupt the tolerant immunologic environment required for pregnancy.

optionExplanations.A: Phenylalanine is metabolized through a different amino-acid pathway.
optionExplanations.B: Cholesterol is central to steroid and lipid metabolism but is not the IDO1 substrate.
optionExplanations.C: Tyrosine is not the substrate of IDO1.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. IDO1 metabolizes tryptophan.
optionExplanations.E: Glucose is handled by carbohydrate metabolic pathways, not IDO1.

questions.takeaway: IDO1 = tryptophan metabolism at the maternal-fetal interface.
questions.recognition: IDO1 questions should trigger “tryptophan depletion/tolerance.”

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child has a progressive neurologic disorder requiring a feeding tube, mobility equipment, frequent specialist visits, and repeated hospitalizations. The family asks whether adding palliative care means they must stop disease-directed therapy. Which response is most accurate?
options: Palliative care is appropriate only during the final 48 hours of life
Palliative care requires discontinuation of all specialist care
Palliative care is limited to prescribing opioid analgesics
Palliative care can be offered only after hospice enrollment
Palliative care can be integrated with ongoing treatment to improve quality of life for the child and family
questions.hint: Do not confuse palliative care with hospice. One can begin much earlier and alongside treatment.
questions.explanation: Palliative care is appropriate for patients with serious, complex illness and can be incorporated alongside disease-directed treatment. In children with medical complexity, integrating palliative care can improve quality of life by addressing symptoms, communication, psychosocial needs, family support, and care coordination.

optionExplanations.A: Palliative care is not limited to the final hours or days of life.
optionExplanations.B: Palliative care complements rather than replaces specialist and disease-directed care.
optionExplanations.C: Palliative care addresses far more than analgesia, including symptoms, communication, psychosocial support, and family needs.
optionExplanations.D: Hospice enrollment is not required before palliative care can be provided.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Palliative care can be integrated concurrently with ongoing treatment.

questions.takeaway: Palliative care can occur alongside disease-directed therapy; hospice is a narrower end-of-life model.
questions.recognition: If the question implies “palliative = giving up,” the correct response is usually that palliative care can be concurrent with treatment.
